1131825,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.2,1938-02-07,72301392-358f-43d7-8b68-608085a933ee,ca.m.2287,Mr. A. A. BROWN (Hamilton East):,,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,"Mr. Speaker, during the week-end while I was home certain merchants and manufacturers in and about the city of Hamilton called upon me, and in the course of our conversation advised me that two of the greatest factors that were contributing to the unemployment situation and to increasing unemployment to-day in that district were, first, that American
The Address-Mr. Brown

goods are being dumped into our markets at much below the selling price in the United States, and, second, that a flood of Japanese goods are being sold in the departmental and retail stores of this country, to an extent which is hardly realized by the general public. The Japanese have gone into making screws, brushes, book-ends, lighters, etc., many of which articles are selling in Canada at much below the cost even of the materials that enter into them. It simply means that these industries in Japan are being subsidized by the people of Canada, and, I repeat, they are selling their goods in this country at a price below or at best equal to the cost of the materials used in producing them.

Before the house adjourned on Friday, I was saying that it seems to me that the government is too well satisfied with the present financial and social conditions in this country. To such an extent is this true that you can read the speech from the throne as often as you like, and you will find in it no indication of any measures proposed to reduce the uncontrollable expenditure, which accounts for some forty cents out of every dollar of revenue collected. No measures are being taken to wipe out the sugar tax, which the members of this government, when in opposition, opposed so strenuously, and there is no suggestion that the eight per cent sales tax is to be reduced, although it is one of the chief obstacles to carrying on business in this country. Nor is there suggested any practical scheme of cooperation with the provinces and municipalities to remove from real estate the tremendous burden of taxation from which it is suffering, and which is the great obstacle to a revival of the building industry. I think if the government would make some effort to cooperate with these other governing bodies it would do much more to help the building industry than the present financial loan arrangements for that same purpose.

Another year has passed, Mr. Speaker, and no measure has been introduced by this government to deal effectively with our railway problem, which has been increasing the national debt by many millions of dollars year after year. The railway problem, I think it is generally recognized, is one of the most important with which this country has to deal, and speaking for myself I do not think we shall have any major degree of prosperity until this problem is solved.

Perusing the speech from the throne we find that the government's idea of a substantial measure of social reform consists of a proposed amendment to the British North America Act which would enable parliament

to enact forthwith a national scheme of unemployment insurance. Such a measure, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most important with which this .parliament could be called upon to deal, and I fear that the government is not attaching to it the importance it deserves. It is a measure that would affect to a very great extent my constituency of Hamilton East. Hamilton is one of the largest industrial cities of this dominion. It is situated in one of the richest fruit and vegetable growing districts, the prosperity of which is dependent upon the millions of dollars paid out annually in wages by the industries in the Hamilton district. There is no part of the country more sensitive to fluctuations and variations in industry than Hamilton and the surrounding district, and uncertainty as to the attitude of this government in the matter of making tariffs and making treaties has contributed to unemployment there.

The government appears to have adopted the attitude that it took between the years 1921 and 1930, when it reduced the tariff, without any compensating benefits to the people of this country, at a time when all the other nations of the world were raising tariffs. When the members on this side of the house complained about the grave injuries that were being done to our industries by these tariff reductions, hon. gentlemen opposite pointed then, as they do to-day, to our huge external trade and to the large revenues that are being collected; they closed their eyes entirely to the fact that hundreds of thousands of Canadians were leaving Canada to look for work in the United States. Following the tariff reductions made during that period, various products that were manufactured in the many branch factories in Hamilton were no longer manufactured there but were manufactured in the main factory in the United States. But when the Conservative party came into power in 1930 and raised the tariff to ensure that our industries would be able to compete on even terms with those of foreign nations, products that had never before been manufactured in the branch factories in Hamilton were manufactured there, and with very little, if any, increase in price to the consumers.

When the Liberal party came into power again in 1935, we found history repeating itself. The government, in its quest for international trade, is making or contemplating making treaties which according to rumour it is hoped will not sacrifice our industries and will be of benefit to this country.
I do not wish the members of this house to think I believe in the tariff as a panacea
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

for all our economic ills. Nor do I believe in high tariffs. I believe that we must trade with other nations, but I contend that a proper protective tariff in order to influence trade balances, to provide work and opportunities for both the farmer and the industrial worker, is the right tariff for a nation such as ours. It is impossible to have any measure of social or economic reform unless all parties in this house agree to the principle of a fair protective tariff.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Albert A. Brown,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=72301392-358f-43d7-8b68-608085a933ee&Language=E&Section=ALL

1131827,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.4,1938-02-07,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver East):,,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,I find myself in what is no doubt a similar position to that of many other hon. members: we should have liked to see something more in the speech from the throne than there is in it, yet we are not greatly disappointed, because we did not expect it.

But there are certain things that we have a right to expect. This is the third session of parliament since this government came into office, and we have the right to expect that the government, possessing as it does the power, should give effect to some of the promises it made to the electorate before it assumed office. The government should not forget that it is here to-day because of a failure of the former government to deal effectively with the economic situation. It should also be remembered that this government came into office at a very much more favourable time than the former administration. The previous government came into office when the country was going into the deeps of the depression, a depression not peculiar to this country but common to the world at large; whereas the present government came into power when the economic situation the world over was improving. They are therefore more accountable to the people of Canada than was the former government because they have not extended that improvement to a larger section of the population. I am not taking up the cudgels on behalf of the previous administration; we criticized them as we criticize the present one, but there is that difference, and it should be remembered.

It is true that some improvement has taken place since this government came into office, but it cannot be denied that the government is not responsible for that improvement, because a similar process has been going on all over the world, and great as is the power of this government it does not extend much beyond the bounds of the dominion.

In my opinion there is a reason why more has not been done, and until that reason is recognized and considered, very little will be done. It is that, underlying the economic fluctuations of to-day not only in Canada but all over the world, there is a fundamental flaw in the economic system itself. The circumstances and conditions which built up in the past what we were pleased to call prosperity have disappeared and will not return. As I have said, the improvement of which we boast has been world-wide. The depression, of which we already see signs, will also be world-wide. And no country in the world has made less preparation to meet it than Canada has.

When the parts'- now in power went to the people in 1935, it presented a fairly definite program, with planks dealing with various matters of concern to the people. Chief among these was unemployment, and the Liberal party promised to deal effectively with it. The improved economic conditions in the last two and a half years have of course diminished unemployment, but let us remember that in one month alone, last December, over

column2: were added to the unemployed lists, and there is nothing in the policies of this government that could have prevented that occurrence. Similar increases, brought about by a world-wide situation, may take place in the coming months, and all the improvement, as far as employment is concerned, would be wiped away.

column1: Then we were promised unemployment insurance. I am pleased that the government is taking steps to give effect to that pledge, but I was astonished the other day when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that the actions of the former-Conservative- government were responsible for this delay of five years. Unemployment insurance was a plank in the Liberal party's platform as far back as 1919. If that be so, and it is so, the Liberal government of to-day is responsible for a delay of fourteen years.

We were also promised the liberation of external trade. Trade of course has increased. This government said not only that it would improve conditions by enlarging trade within empire countries but that it would increase trade with all countries. The facts are otherwise. I have before me an article by Courtland Elliott in Canadian Business, the official organ of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. It is pointed out, in an analysis of Canadian trade, that our trade with the United Kingdom is, in percentages, approximately the same as it was in 1932; that is,
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
taking the months January to October, 1932, and comparing them with the months January to October, 1937.

1131833,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.10,1938-02-07,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. MacINNIS:,,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,I thought I had made that clear; I am sorry that I did not. Our total trade with the United States has increased by some nine per cent. The percentage of our total trade with empire countries, that is the British dominions, increased by a very small amount, but the percentage of our total trade with other foreign countries decreased from 22-3 per cent to 11-6 per cent. That is not extending trade on the basis on which the government promised it would be extended.
Then we were promised control of credit. I have a copy of the Liberal platform, which has a note on the back saying:
The paragraphs above have been extracted from the official report of Mr. Mackenzie King's speech in the House of Commons, on February 27, 1933.
With regard to the control of credit the following statement is made:
The Liberal party believes that credit is a
ublic matter, not of interest to bankers only,
ut of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank . . .

And so on. In this regard there has been no change that has had any significance whatever; and for that statement I have no less an authority than the hon. member for Vancouver r-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). Speaking at the annual meeting of the Vancouver-Burrard Liberal Association on November 4, he said, as reported in the Daily Province:

Government control of the Bank of Canada for the benefit of the people has been promised by the Liberal party, said Mr. McGeer, and he for one would not sit idly in his seat at Ottawa without protesting that it be put into effect.

That would seem to be conclusive evidence that this plank at least has not been carried into effect. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is an authority on monetary reform. I know he is an authority because he has said so himself. He used to talk a good deal about it and spread enlightenment in regard to this very complex subject, but he does not do so any more.

May I take this opportunity also to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) on the attitude he took in the trouble that developed at Oshawa last year. I intend to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett); I shall vote for it, but I should be much
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

more enthusiastic about it if it were more positive and less negative than it is. If it had stated the lines along which the Conservative party would proceed to lay the foundation of an enduring prosperity I would vote for it with far more enthusiasm than I shall when the vote is taken.

Two facts stand out in the life of Canada to-day; we have a country of great potential wealth, vast possibilities, and we have a country in which there is dire poverty. And the poverty of the masses is increasing; the poverty of the farmers, despite supposed improvement in the last few years, is increasing. We should try to find out the fundamental cause of this situation. Surely it is not because the wealth is not here or because our people are not prepared to work and produce wealth; there must be some other difficulty, some other fundamental cause that we have not discovered. There has been, of course, very little attempt to deal scientifically with the economic and social questions confronting us, and I submit they are not incapable of solution if we approach them in a scientific way. The small group to which I have the honour to belong believes that the solution lies in the methods which we have suggested in this house and elsewhere during the last few years. Why is it that to-day we have such enormous aggregations of capital in the banks-capital unemployed? Why is it that to-day the banks have such enormous investments in our securities? Is there lack of confidence in our ability properly to function as a producing country?

Indeed honesty should go much further. It should cause him to resign his seat and give the people who elected him on the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation program an opportunity to approve or disapprove his

action. However, there was method in his silence. When he left the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation he with a few others formed a new party, the Social Constructive party. He no doubt hoped that when he came here this session he would be able to announce himself as the spearhead of a real socialist political movement in Canada. Things however do not always turn out as we wish. His party was absolutely rejected by the electorate of British Columbia, and no longer exists. He has therefore come to the profound conclusion that he is definitely of the ""Liberal structure of mind"", and sees no reason why the Liberal party should not open its ranks to him. I agree with him in that respect; I think he is Tory enough to find an abiding resting place in the Liberal fold. But when he says that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in British Columbia is not a coherent group, and no longer represents a truly foundational opposition to the existing so-called capitalist party, I do not agree with him, because the facts are all to the contrary. Despite the opposition of the old parties, and the party of which my hon. friend was a member, we maintained our numerical strength in the British Columbia legislature, and it is an accepted fact that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group was very coherent and the only effective opposition in the British Columbia legislature during the recent session. If the hon. member for Nanaimo does not know these facts he should read the British Columbia press, preferably with an open mind.

With much of what my hon. friend had to say regarding the communist party I agree. That party does try to get into and control other organizations, political, industrial and social. That policy, however, is not confined to this country. The way to overcome the machinations of the communist party is to oppose them, not to run away as my hon. friend did. We also know that the British Columbia section of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation dealt definitely and decisively with the communist party at its last convention in July, 1937.

Why did my hon. friend raise the communist bogey? A short excerpt from the speech which he quoted the other evening, his maiden speech of 1936, will give a clue to what he had in mind. I quote from his speech on that occasion, referring to Hansard at page 182:

But, sir, I do ask this honourable house and its members not to confuse the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group of seven with those who in present day colloquial speech are classed as communists and anarchists. To do that is all too common; but if you must do it, it will not ultimately harm us.
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
May I say to my hon. friend, as he said then, that if he must do it, it will not ultimately harm us. He continued:

Nearly two thousand years ago those who followed the Master heard the term "" Christian "" spoken in utter opprobrium, and it did not hurt his followers. But these terms are intended by many in the house and all through the country to bring into derision the cause we uphold.

Nothing more need be said in regard to that, but my hon. friend's closing remarks when dealing with this subject the other night were truly pathetic in their transparency. He said, quoting from page 166 of Hansard:

So it is that while still a socialist I declare that I am essentially of the liberal structure of mind, and while my election in 1935 constrains me to call myself an independent for the time being I recognize the weakness to the country and my people in the stand I am constrained to take. I definitely believe that there are many not only potential but essential socialists in the Liberal and Conservative ranks, and I believe it would be to the advantage of the country and its progress if the leaders of the old line parties would declare their readiness to embrace all proper to their particular structure of mind, no matter how their intelligence and purpose may desire constitutionally to vary the country's present economy and economic social system.
Out of this statement the following syllogism emerges:

column2: I am a socialist of the liberal structure of mind.""
The leaders of the old parties should embrace people of their particular structure.""
Therefore the leader of the Liberal party should embrace me.""

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to discuss a number of questions which have been raised in the course of the debate I should like to add my congratulations to those already extended by other members of the house to the mover and the seconder of the address. It was quite evident, I think, from the high quality of their speeches, that they will add considerably to the strength of the government benches, and I believe it was equally evident that both the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Francoeur) and the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) will bring honour and distinction to the constituencies which they represent in this parliament.
I hope my hon. friend who has just spoken will forgive me if I do not follow him in the course of his argument. I shall have occasion
fMr. Maclnnis.]
a little later to take issue with him in some of his conclusions.

On Monday of last week I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech delivered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It did seem to me at the time that this speech was a mixture of righteous indignation and unrighteous criticism. I thought then, and I still think, that some of t'he statements and charges made in the course of that speech went much beyond the amenities of parliamentary debate, and I feel quite sure that members of the house who have had a longer experience of parliamentary discussion than I have had would share that impression with me.

Some of the thunderbolts of my right hon. friend were directed against persons outside of this house, who are not in a position to defend themselves; some were directed against individual members of the government, including myself. In dealing with the subject matter of some of these charges, as I propose to do a little later, I should like to make it quite clear to the house at the outset that I do not do so with any desire for immunity from criticism or with any feeling that any special importance should be attached to questions of personal vindication. Criticism is a legitimate and necessary function of the opposition under our parliamentary system, and it follows as a matter of course that the leader of the opposition must have the utmost freedom in his comments on any and every aspect of government policy. Nevertheless it is equally clear, I believe, that freedom of this kind is almost certain to be abused unless it is restrained by a sense of responsibility, and I do not think it is going too far to say that in the course of his speech on Monday last my right hon. friend did exceed the limits of legitimate criticism.

Perhaps it would be idle to speculate on the motives which led him to indulge in his tirade of suspicion, rumour and denunciation, but it did occur to me at the time that he might wish to create a diversion-I think that is the military term-in order to cover his retreat from Winnipeg to Edmonton; his movement, so to speak, from the old Conservative policy of 1928 to the new Conservative policy of 1938. My right hon. friend has had some experience in changing direction suddenly, but I cannot help but believe that he would wish to execute this manoeuvre behind a smoke screen of some kind, because otherwise it might appear that he, the commander, was some distance ahead of his army, or it might even appear that he had no army at all. But all these are questions, of course, on which I cannot hope to speak with authority.
The Address-Mr. Rogers

Before dealing with some of the charges made by the leader of the opposition I believe it will meet with the wishes of hon. members on both sides of this house if I review briefly the unemployment situation and the figures with respect to relief, in the light of developments which have taken place during the past year. As announced in the speech from the throne, there has been a marked increase in employment and a marked decrease in the numbers of those receiving unemployment aid. I am sure that statement in the speech from the throne was received with general satisfaction. As a matter of fact, I think it is fair to say that it is a very moderate statement of the improvement that has taken place during the past year, and particularly during the six months from April to October.

As members of the house are aware, there has been some criticism in the past owing to the lack of comparability in the figures respecting the number of those on relief. Fortunately we are now in a position where we can say that there is strict comparability, so far as comparisons of last year and the year previous are concerned. The registration conducted by the national employment commission began in September, 1936, and has continued steadily from that time forward. The figures which I propose to give to the house and which will illustrate the improvement which has taken place during the past year are figures from the registration conducted by the national employment commission.

I think it is well to explain that there is an unavoidable time lag in the publication of figures from the registration of those on relief. It will be readily understood that the figures for October cannot be sent in by the municipalities and provinces all across the dominion until after the end of the month or some time early in November. It is equally clear that these figures cannot be assembled and analyzed without some loss of time. At the same time I am pleased, however, to be able to say to the house that the delay has been decreased and we are hoping for a still further improvement as time goes on.

The usefulness of the registration has been amply revealed by our experience during the past fifteen months. For example, it enables us to measure the changing trends in the unemployment situation from month to month. It also enables us to measure seasonal variations with respect to particular sections of the dominion. This has been of considerable importance in dealing with problems of transiency of the single unemployed and also in

the formulation of projects suitable to different sections of the country under the appropriation for youth training. Finally, it has been of great importance in connection with our periodic revision of grants in aid.

Apart from these advantages, which after all concern administration, I think it is fair to say that the usefulness of the registration of the unemployed on relief has become quite evident in another direction. The time was when we were confronted with these staggering figures of millions or hundreds of thousands and were left with the impression that they represented the total of those who were actually employable and unemployed in this country. I have even seen this suggestion in some newspaper editorials and I was very much surprised to note that the actual figures had not been analyzed more carefully before such a suggestion was created. However, through the registration, through bulletins issued by the national employment commission and through press releases, I believe there is now throughout the country a much more accurate appreciation of the problem of unemployment and relief.

We have been able, so to speak, to separate the total problem into its constituent elements of social and economic significance. We now make a distinction in our thinking between those who are receiving agricultural assistance and those who are receiving unemployment aid. We now make a distinction between those who are employable and those who are unemployable. We also make a distinction between those who are dependent and on relief and those who are heads of families or who are individuals capable of employment. As I have suggested, all this has given us a better appreciation of the problem itself and a clearer recognition of the definite progress that has been made, particularly during the past year, in the absorption by private industry of very large numbers of those who were employable and on relief.

I think I can best convey the improvement in the employment situation, and its reflection in the reduction of relief rolls in the industrial areas, by giving a summary of the completed figures of registration for the month of October. As I have suggested, these figures are comparable with the figures for October, 1936. The registration conducted by the national employment commission began in September of that year. I might say that the complete figures for November, 1937, and the preliminary figures for December will be available in a few days.
The Address-Mr. Rogers

First of all, there is the material aid given to persons other than resident farm operators. I want to emphasize the distinction between agricultural assistance and unemployment aid because, after all, agricultural assistance is a different problem. Agricultural distress is mainly due to climatic causes and cannot be attributed in a large way to the operation of economic factors or policies. The reduction in the dominion total of recipients of unemployment aid in October, 1937, as compared with October, 1936, was 44-3 per cent. The decrease in the dominion total of partially employable persons in the same year was 23-5 per cent, and the decrease in the dominion total of unemployables was 9-4 per cent. The decrease in the grand total of non-agricultural aid recipients, including individuals and heads of families and their dependents, amounted to 36-7 per cent.

I turn next to those in receipt of agricultural aid. In the year under review the decrease in the total of farmers and their families, other than in the province of Saskatchewan, receiving aid, amounted to 71-3 per cent. This decrease is a clear reflection of the improvement in crop conditions in most of the provinces of the dominion, and it also brings home to us the serious disaster which

has befallen Saskatchewan during the past year. The increase in the total of farmers and their families in Saskatchewan receiving agricultural aid was 95-3 per cent. The increase in the total for all provinces of those receiving agricultural aid was 22-4 per cent.

I come now to all classes receiving material aid, that is, those receiving unemployment aid and those receiving agricultural assistance. From October, 1936, to October, 1937, there has been a net decrease of 20-3 per cent. Perhaps I might also give a summary of the preliminary figures for November of this year as compared with November of 1936. It would seem that the figures for fully employable persons will still be about 40 per cent below those for November of the previous year. There has been an increase of about ten per cent over October, 1937, in the total number of persons receiving aid, but this change is one that we would have anticipated because of the variations in seasonal employment. There has been a decrease of 15-7 peT cent, as compared with November, 1936, in the total of all classes receiving aid.

1131880,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.57,1938-02-07,28eb2ff4-b1a9-437b-87d1-34c64f68f258,ca.m.7788,Mr. ROGERS:,Minister of Labour,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,I ask my right hon. friend to read it more carefully, for I concluded as much myself. My views on the tariff can be expressed very simply. The tariff is an instrument of policy. If it is used at all other than for purposes of revenue in a federal state it should be used with due regard to its effect upon the maintenance of national unity. Where you have a situation such as exists in Australia and Canada, where secondary industries are largely concentrated in two provinces and where primary and export industries are largely concentrated in other provinces, you cannot move to extremes in tariff policy without endangering national unity and without undermining the very foundations of federal public finance. A high tariff policy will threaten national unity, and no one ought to know it better than the leader of the opposition. Similarly, whatever may have been possible sixty years ago, the abolition of tariffs at this time would disrupt confederation. In any realistic view of our present situation the course of wisdom is the course of moderation.

But while we retain a tariff system I submit that we should keep constantly in mind that there are seven provinces in this dominion whose income is supplied very largely, in some provinces almost exclusively, by primary and export industries, and we must be willing also to study the unequal incidence of the tariff and be prepared to apply such compensating adjustments as may be practicable. That is the position which I developed before the royal commission of economic enquiry in Nova Scotia. That is the position which I hold to-day. It is a position which, I believe, is entirely con-
The Address-Mr. Rogers
sistent with Liberal policy. It is a position which is entirely inconsistent with the traditional policy of the Conservative party.

In this connection let me remind the leader of the opposition that this present administration has already recognized the claims of primary and export industries in three directions. It has reduced the duties on implements of production. It has concluded a reciprocity agreement with the United States which has conferred special benefits on those provinces which have suffered most from the incidence of the protective system. And it has revised and renewed the Ottawa agreements with the same object in view, even though the negotiation of these several agreements did involve the lessening of protection of some of our secondary industries. Finally, this administration has appointed a royal commission to make a thorough inquiry into the whole structure of federal public finance. If the leader of the opposition has any doubts as to the validity of these conclusions which were presented to the Nova Scotia commission of economic inquiry, I would remind him that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in their brief presented to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, recognized in effect that the tariff had been unequal in its incidence and suggested the wisdom of some compensating adjustments.

column2: The unequal effects between states are probably the most embarrassing consequences of the tariff, but they have their roots in the unequal effects between industries, which are natural and inevitable consequences of tariff protection. 1131909,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.86,1938-02-07,28eb2ff4-b1a9-437b-87d1-34c64f68f258,ca.m.7788,Mr. ROGERS:,Minister of Labour,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,I promise to be brief. I wish to refer to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition in his speech on Monday last. That amendment is in the following terms:

We desire respectfully to express regret that the speech from the throne does not indicate that the government have taken or contemplate taking efficient measures to deal with unfavourable economic conditions in Canada, and that no legislative action is proposed to deal effectively with the prevailing uncertainty and insecurity resulting from the inadequate incomes of large numbers of our people.

I should like to say first that the figures I was able to quote a while ago with respect to the improvement in employment made it abundantly clear that during the past year there was in fact a remarkable improvement not merely in the number of wage earners in this country but also in the number of those who previously had been in receipt of state relief but are now happily earning incomes of their own. As a matter of fact, in the period under review some 95,000 have moved from relief rolls into employment in private industry. These men and women are earning incomes where previously they were bn relief. Not only that, but if one takes the latest available figures from the bureau of statistics, as of December, giving the estimate of unemployment in Canada, and carries the statistics back to 1930, the following is shown:
Estimate of Unemployment in Canada
December-

In other words, during the past year there has been an improvement to the extent of 120,000. I should explain to the house that these figures include those who have been unemployed but not upon relief. The earlier figure I gave of 95,000 covers only those who previously had been on relief.

It might also be pertinent I think to place before the house the actual improvement in wages and earnings which has taken place during the past year. Wage rates during 1936 and 1937 have continued the recovery from the low level of 1933, so that the index number for 1937 was only 2-7 per cent lower than in 1930. It was 11 per cent lower in 1935, and in 1933 it was 15 per cent lower. The greatest recovery has been in logging and saw-milling, which had an increase of 13 per cent over 1936, making the level for 1937 nearly 24 per cent higher than in 1935 and 55 per cent higher than in 1933. In manufac-

turing industries the increase in 1937 was 8 per cent over 1936 and 16 per cent over 1933. The industries showing the greatest increases during the year were: automobile manufacturing, 15 per cent; cotton, 11 per cent; meat packing, 19 per cent; pulp and paper, 12 per cent; crude iron and steel, 14 per cent; metal trades, 10 per cent. Wages in the building trades, which fell 24 per cent between 1930 and 1934, have risen nearly 7 per cent but are still 18 per cent lower than in 1930. On steam railways the rates were only 4 per cent below 1930 in December, and the reductions will be fully restored by April 1 of this year. On electric street railways and in printing trades and coal mining the reductions were less but increases are gradually being made. The principal coal mines in Nova Scotia raised wages nearly ten per cent in 1937.

Moreover, earnings of employees have shown considerable increases. On the principal steam railways, for the first eleven months of 1937 the total compensation paid was $160,419,196 as compared with $152,334,902 in the same period in 1936, and $144,751,921 in 1935. This is the only industry for which earnings of employees in 1937 are available. Figures for certain manufacturing industries for 1936 have been issued. In the primary iron and steel industry the total earnings of employees in 1936 were $13,830,377 as compared with $12,279,390 in 1935 and $14,934,325 in 1930. In petroleum refining, earnings in 1936 were $7,193,148 as compared with $7,046,675 in 1935, $5,897,811 in 1932 and $8,190,130 in 1930. In the men's clothing industry earnings in 1936 were $10,255,745 as compared with $8,990,370 in 1935 and $11,542,990 in 1930.

These figures cover only a very limited part of industry throughout Canada, but they are representative and illustrate the very marked improvement in wages and earnings which has taken place during the past year.

In the light of the improvement which has taken place since the present government came into office, the expanding trade, the expanding income, the expanding employment., the expanding revenues, and the declining deficits, it does seem to me that there is every reason why this house should give its confidence to this administration, even as that confidence has been given in abundant measure by the people of this country.

MacNICOL (Davenport):,,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the remarks made by the various speakers, unless time permits me to refer to some of the last remarks made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who has just sat down, particularly his remarks in regard to unemployment insurance.
The Address-Mr. MacNicol
I want to deal first with the second sentence in paragraph 4 of the speech from the throne, which reads:
Trade with other countries has materially expanded.

With every hon. member of the house I rejoice when the trade of Canada expands, particularly if it expands along sound economic lines. Experienced business men, however, in trying to obtain more customers for that which they produce, are very careful not to alienate the loyalty of dependable customers of long standing. I claim that is exactly what this government has done, in one particular in any event, and I have time only to deal with that one particular. I refer to the anthracite coal trade. The government are so infatuated with such expressions as ""expanding trade"" and ""trade expansion"" that in my judgment they have made a very grievous error in their handling of the Welsh anthracite coal trade which may mean the loss of considerable trade to Canada in the form of produce shipped in return to Wales and, in a smaller degree, to Scotland, where we also obtain anthracite coal.

It was an incident that occurred last June in Wales, where I had gone to make my own survey of the ramifications of the anthracite coal trade, that made me determine to refer to the matter in the house on the very first available occasion. I had been asked to address a meeting of coal producers, following a dinner, in the Metropole hotel at Swansea. Just before I rose to speak a porter came into the room and handed a clipping, which I hold in my hand, to the chairman of the meeting, who afterwards handed it to me. I may say that it was on June 7 that I was at Swansea, and this clipping is dated Ottawa, May 29, containing a quotation from the Montreal Standard of that date:

Almost a whole year in advance of the next federal budget, the advance guard of the coal lobby has taken up its position on parliament hill, determined that it will succeed before another session is past in its objective of having the existing duties abolished against American anthracite and bituminous coals.
Further the quotation states:
Ontario is credited with being the chief sufferer under the existing tariffs, with Quebec bearing the balance of the burden.

The newspaper clipping does not reveal the names of any of the lobbyists, but I am satisfied that there would be none from either Nova Scotia or Alberta. I cannot speak for Quebec, but so far as Ontario is concerned I believe I can say that the people of this province are willing, and indeed glad, to give a preference to Nova Scotia bituminous coal, wherever 51952-144

it can be used, as against foreign bituminous coal. Likewise I believe they are glad to give a preference to Alberta coal, wherever it can be used, and to Welsh and Scotch anthracite in the importations we have to make.

Ten or fifteen years ago Canada regularly imported approximately five million tons of anthracite coal per year, all of it from the United States. Then, I claim through the good judgment of members of the house, irrespective of party, legislation or regulations, were initiated to encourage bringing Nova Scotia bituminous coal to Ontario and Quebec, as well as Alberta coal to Saskatchewan, Manitoba and northwestern Ontario. As a result our importations of anthracite coal were reduced from five million tons to three and a half million tons, at which point they seem to be fairly well established.

When the government of the present right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came into power, he implemented his promise to the electorate to increase intra-empire trade, in large degree in connection with the importation of Welsh anthracite, and in substantial degree in connection with the importation of Scotch anthracite. In fact he carried out that promise in many ways, but time will permit me to deal only with this one. Let us see what the situation was as far as the importation of anthracite was concerned when the right hon. gentleman formed his government. In 1929, the last full year during which the previous government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in power, Canada imported 3,173,043 tons of American anthracite coal and 729,458 tons of Welsh anthracite coal. There was no Scotch anthracite imported that year. In 1934, the last full year of the government of the right hon. gentleman, thanks to his policy of increasing trade between the different parts of the empire, the situation had changed. Just here may I say that I know of no trade that is carried on with greater benefit to both the exporter and the importer than the importation of Welsh and Scotch anthracite coal in exchange for Canadian farm produce. In the last full year of the former Conservative government, 1934, importations of United States anthracite coal fell to 1,804,127 tons, while importations of Welsh anthracite increased to 1,334,517 tons. We brought in also 309,000 tons of Scotch coal, making a total importation of United Kingdom anthracite amounting to 1,643,517 tons, or not much less than the amount we imported from the United States.
What has happened to this fine trade, as a result of the ""expanding trade"" policy of the
The Address-Mr. MacNicol

present government, without regard to whether or not tried and true customers are alienated? Last year, 1937, Canada imported from the United States 1,888,860 tons of anthracite, while our total importation of Scotch and Welsh coal was reduced to 1,123,841 tons. At the same time we imported 264,048 tons from Germany, 146,648 tons from Russia, 19,000 tons from Indo-China and 20,000 tons from Belgium. In other words our total importation of foreign anthracite last year was 2,338,000 tons, while our total importation of United Kingdom coal fell to 1,123,841 tons.

An examination of these figures surely will reveal why there is a marked and rising resentment in Wales to-day in regard to Canada's anthracite coal policy. If that resentment continues I feel certain that it will be reflected in a greatly reduced number of return cargoes of Canadian farm products. For the life of me I cannot see what the government expects to gain by reducing our importations of anthracite coal from the United Kingdom by 500,000 tons and then going all over the face of the earth, to countries to which we cannot possibly ship our farm produce, in order to bring in 500,000 tons of coal to make up the difference. Personally I would much rather deal with tried and true customers like Wales and Scotland in an exchange of this kind, which is beneficial to all concerned, than go all over the face of the earth in an attempt to expand our trade, in any event in connection with this particular commodity.

A few moments ago I said that last June I made a rather extended survey of the situation in Wales. I went through the mining areas and visited many of the mines. I imagine that every one in Canada has been touched by the newspaper reports which have appeared from time to time describing the distress in the Welsh coal mining areas as a result of the reduction in exportations of coal. In my judgment it is small business on the part of this government to inflict further distress upon Wales through a reduction in the importations of coal from Wales as well as from Scotland. When visiting the different coal mining towns I saw a number of bills similar to the one I hold in my hand. These were pasted up in the different stores from which the miners purchased their supplies, but I am afraid that they will be taken down before very long. I might say that Canada's purchases of Welsh coal gave employment to 7,000 miners, and her purchases of Scotch coal gave employment to as many as 2,000 miners. These bills, which were printed both in English and in Welsh were very illuminating.

These things are disquieting to the Scotch and Welsh buyers of Canadian products, and I find that there is a depressed feeling in the situation as far as coal exporters are concerned. Before leaving for the old country I went to see some of the coal importers in Toronto from whom I buy Nova Scotia and Welsh coal. They told me that the price of Welsh coal was perhaps a little high in Canada because of the breakage or ""degradation"" in shipping. They referred to the breakagesaving equipment used by German shippers. In order to make a thorough investigation of this matter I visited Rotterdam and Antwerp, the ports from which German coal is shipped. I also inspected the docks at Swansea. I got many good photographs of the equipment used in loading German coal. I was told that the ministry of industries in Germany, to which I shall refer a little later on, subsidizes the exportation of German products. I do not know whether the German government have paid any part of the cost of the equipment at Rotterdam or Antwerp,
but I would not be surprised to learn that they had. I understand a large sum of money was voted last year for the encouragement of exports.

At Antwerp and Rotterdam there are four lines of railroad tracks on the docks parallel to the ships. This means that at least four different kinds of coal can be loaded into a ship at the same time. The latest type of crane is used with which to take the coal from the cars and place it in the hold of the ship. The net result is that the breakage or ""degradation"" is quite small. At Swansea the cars come singly to the ship and at right angles. The car is lifted on an elevator and tilted over and sometimes the coal is dropped twenty, forty or sixty feet into the hold of the ship. At other times it is dropped on an escalator. The equipment at Swansea is not equal to what they have at Antwerp and Rotterdam.

I submit that this government should initiate a national or an empire coal policy and take some steps to try to improve the method of shipping Welsh coal. This might be done, first, through approaching the British government; second, through approaching the railroads; third, through approaching the producers and, fourth, the shippers. In this way the ""degradation"" or breakage of Welsh coal in shipment might be reduced, with a corresponding decrease in the Canadian price of the coal.

1131933,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.11.110,1938-02-07,449e1e87-7c70-4086-bf84-ce748397efe9,ca.m.4901,Mr. CHARLES PARENT (Quebec West and South) (Translation):,,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,,Mr. Speaker, I do not wish needlessly to delay the vote on the address by a long speech, but I do not think it would be imposing on the kindness of the house to offer one or two observations, first, on the subject of civil liberty in Quebec, and next, on the advisability of beautifying Quebec city and preserving its historic character by extending the authority of the national battlefields commission over certain federal properties. Before broaching these subjects, however, may I tender my most sincere congratulations to the honourable members who proposed and seconded the motion. This oratorical classic always bears a stamp of its own. Whether it is to seek relaxation from patronage troubles, I cannot say, but it is undeniable that practically all members of the house follow attentively when these speeches are delivered. In addition, the galleries are filled with members of the fair sex, belonging to fashionable Canadian society for whom the social events of the Capital have much interest at this season. The task of the mover and seconder of the address is therefore a heavy one, Mr. Speaker, and the entire house rejoices at the success obtained.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to some honourable members who have upbraided the government because, in the speech from the throne, no reference was made to the civil rights of our people. I may point out to the house that nowhere in the world do civilized people enjoy more freedom and tolerance than they do in the province of Quebec. In Quebec city, where I live, there are several thousand English-speaking protestants. We are all living in perfect harmony. Moreover, we see, withm a distance of a few hundred feet, the catholic and the protestant cathedrals, and every Sunday we witness the edifying spectacle of catholic French-Canadians and protestant English speaking people wending their way together towards their respective place of worship, mutually respectful of their religious belief, with never a clash or a display of unfriendliness. We speak of them as they speak of us, with the utmost regard. We respect their pastors, just as they respect our priests.

Since the days of Jogues, Brebeuf and Lallemand, three centuries of history have recorded the devotion, the sacrifices and the wonderful deeds accomplished in our country in the name of Faith. That constitutes the very basis of our existence. No wonder that those who preach among us the non-existence of God should be branded as barbarians.

I take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the government the great national eucharistic congress which will take place in Quebec next summer. I do hope the government will vote an appropriation towards the expenses of the congress and that a federal delegate will attend it.

In order to make my speech shorter, Mr. Speaker, I shall take up at once my second point, which is the advisability of providing for the improvement of the city of Quebec and for the preservation of its historic character, by extending to certain federal property the powers of the national battlefields commission. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, not only is Quebec the oldest city in America, but it is also a city of priceless historical treasures. Thanks to the good breeding of its inhabitants, to its narrow streets, to its beautiful climate, to its monuments and its historic associations, Quebec is an interesting place whose quaintness attracts nearly a million tourists every year. It is also the summer residence of His Excellency the Governor General, and for that reason I believe the dominion government should take an especial interest in the improvement of the city. From the rock of Quebec, from that spot which is called Dufferin Terrace, tourists may admire one of the world's most beautiful panoramas. On either shore of the St. Lawrence are to be seen pretty villages whose white cottages stand out against the green mountains, while directly ahead is the island of Orleans which, rising amid the platinum billows of the great river, appears like a gigantic emerald. Mr. Speaker, every time you come to Quebec, I am sure you like to gaze, from that spot, upon some of the most beautiful parishes in your constituency. Perhaps it has occurred to you, as it has to me, that such a wonderful terrace might well be extended toward the west, as far as the National Battlefields park. Besides affording employment, this would provide the most picturesque site in the world.
In 1908, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, realizing the special and national character of Quebec city, appointed the National Battlefields Commission. The purpose of the act whereby that
The Address-Mr Parent
commission was created was to preserve the great battlefields which witnessed the epic struggle between Wolfe and Montcalm, and to restore, in so far as possible, their original features.

In 1911, the dominion government and the transcontinental railway commission acquired several properties and rights of way along the river; to-day these properties and rights of way are quite useless, owing to a change in the location of that railway.

Would it not be advisable, Mr. Speaker, to have these sites under the authority of the battlefields commission or even to have them transferred to it? Would it not be well to extend the commission's jurisdiction so as to include the Quebec walls which are being reconstructed, and, in keeping with our present needs, to lay out public walks as well as to rebuild the old gates which, for the sake of progress, have been destroyed?

In 1928, the dominion government voted an amount of $750,000 to be spread over a period of ten years, and the last payment is due this year. I hope that Laurier's plan may be followed up for many more years and that further appropriations may be voted for the improvement and conservation of that historic site in the oldest city of America. May I express the wish that the extension of the terrace, the general improvement of the city of Quebec and the preservation of its historic sites will have the support of those who, up to this day, have shown their judgment.

Mr. Speaker, I am confident that, with the strong support of my colleagues from Quebec city, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), my humble suggestion will be welcome. It is not only in the interest of Quebec city that I am making it, but also in the interest of the many visitors who come there from across the line. These visitors from abroad are very much impressed when they see Quebec for the first time, for it recalls many memories of the last three centuries, and it has been said of Quebec, that each stone reminds you of the past.

Mr. Speaker, it may be suggested that I make an appeal in behalf of my city and my constituency. In reply, I could quote these words of a writer: ""One is always entitled to speak of his town when he loves it to the very depths of his heart.""

Since I have yet a few minutes to spare, may I be allowed to draw the attention of the government to the fact that those conditions ought to be improved because Quebec is the oldest city in America and our modem needs

were not contemplated in the original plans. Quebec city, owing to its narrow streets and its lack of opportunity for future development, is in a peculiar position regarding the assistance to be given by the dominion government under the housing act. Particularly in my own constituency, where there are many workingmen, several requests did not get from the commission the consideration which they deserved. I hope that the government will see its way clear to have the act amended in order to help the workingman, for, up to now, it has benefited in our part of the country only those who could have built their homes without such assistance. I understand that this legislation is calculated to help those who have not had a very easy life, namely the labourers, our workingmen, who, through their savings, are anxious to provide for a living in their old days. I hope that a representative of the government, after examining the conditions such as they obtain in Quebec, will see fit to put aside a certain tract of land to allow the government to assist in the building of homes where the workingmen, along with those that are in better circumstances, may secure a comfortable life for their children.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
