mind which I think might be illustrated by a quotation from T. B. Macaulay. Some hon. members will remember that in his essay on John Dryden, Macaulay wrote:
His imagination resembled the wings of an ostrich. It enabled him to run, though not to soar.

Sir, the government which it is my privilege to support is in motion; it may be said in many respects to have accelerated its pace to a run but I doubt if it can be said to soar. The return to power of the Liberal party in 1935 was a mandate to give Canada a Liberal government. That was the promise implied in the platform of that party, and that promise was greater and of more importance, to my mind, than the promises of all the leaders of the various parties who met us with opposition at that time. It is not for me to say that the government has failed to give leadership along the Liberal way. We have not failed to make progress, but I think it is my prerogative as a member of the party and a supporter of the government to say to my colleagues in the party at this, the first opportunity I have had in this session, that neither I nor my constituents -many of them, at least-feel that so far we have any great reason to feel smug about the rate of our progress.

We do not differ from other groups in the house with respect to our desire to serve Canada. We do differ as to how that service may be efficiently carried out; or do we? Sometimes one is reminded of the expression, "" By their fruits ye shall know them."" The most damning indictment of the Liberal party is and perhaps always will be that we Liberals are of the same political stripe as our Conservative opponents. Unfortunately, in my opinion during the past three years we have given a measure of hope and courage to our traducers. We hear from our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends not only "" Hear, hear "" but "" We told you so."" Out on the prairies the pool official says "" Me, too,"" and from the shadow of the Rockies, almost out of the ether itself, we hear a voice crying, "" Behold, the lion and the lamb lie down together."" Nobody is fooled, unless we fool ourselves. Sometimes I think we do, we who put through the scandalous furniture tariff changes in the dying moments of the last session; we who in 1930 looked upon the Ottawa agreements with scorn, ostracized the parents and then in 1937 adopted the baby; we who permit the gasoline trust to mulct every user of gasoline on every gallon he uses; we who permit automobile manufacturers to take advantage of all the

engineering developments charged against the American consuming public on their cars and then charge that again here in Canada and, finally, we who permit a Tory tariff board to give advice to our government. That in an individual would be something bordering on treason, and in a political party it is at least foolish.

If that were the whole story there would be much to be desired, but I rejoice that in this ledger there is much to counterbalance and offset it. I do not feel called upon at the moment to deal with the other side; I do not think there is any necessity to stress the achievements of the administration. At the beginning of a session I think perhaps it is a good thing for us to think more particularly about the things that have not been done.

It is perhaps unthinkable, Mr. Speaker, to many minds steeped in the political game, that one should speak out so frankly in this house, but I make no apology for having thought it wise to point out that there is an urge in my mind, as I know there is an urge in the minds of my constituents, to say to the government, "" Faster, faster."" I have a loyalty to the government of the day; that loyalty I give freely, but I also have a loyalty to the hopes and ambitions of the people who are the supporters of this government. I believe in the destiny of Canada; I believe that destiny can be best achieved in the Liberal way, but I want to see it come as quickly as possible along that way.

It is trite to say that these are critical times. It is stressing the obvious to say that the nations are failing to face up to the problems of the day. At this time it is perhaps sufficient to dwell for a little while on the problems peculiarly our own. Perhaps it is a good idea to ask ourselves: What are these great Canadian problems? I suggest, sir, that the first among them is the preservation of Canada herself as a united nation. We in Canada in past years have been much exercised about our national status, our place within the empire. Sometimes I think we have forgotten, too often and for too long a time, to assure ourselves of our own unity. I say quite frankly that if confederation was not an established fact, to-day in Canada it would be impossible. But, sir, seventy years have passed since confederation became an accomplished fact in this country. That union or confederation has been sanctified, if you like, by the blood of thousands of men who died for Canada; not for Quebec or Manitoba or the maritime provinces or British Columbia but for Canada, and the union which has
The Address-Mr. Mutch",,,,
1131937,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.12.1.2,1938-02-07,,,,stagedirection,,,,"stood the stresses and strains of those seventy years must not be permitted to break down under any circumstances.

First of all, we, as members of the House of Commons, are to love and serve Canada, we must know our country. Sometimes when I have come to the city of Ottawa, after I have been here a little while I have felt as I sometimes feel in a little valley high up in the western mountains. After I have been there a while I have an almost overwhelming desire to climb-and I do not like >to climb-to look over the top and see what is going on just beyond that rim which seems so near. Perhaps that feeling of repression in the mountains is the result of having been born on the prairies, but as I come to this parliament hill I sometimes think we are in something of a valley, and we do not see over the edge quite far enough or quite often enough. Perhaps if one did not say the things that come to mind in the first few days of the session, under the influence of that isolation one might refrain altogether from saying them. At any rate if in times past I have been unduly critical of the travelling expenses of any ministers of past governments, I feel like taking it all back and suggesting to those who form the government now, and those yet to come, that they should travel more.

The sectionalism that is so rife-and it is rife-in my opinion is largely the result of ignorance. Ignorance is a greater menace than selfishness, because selfishness is the result of a lack of understanding of our own best interests. Second, there must be leadership, and in Canada we look to this house for that leadership. A member of this house who puts constituency considerations before national considerations should to my mind retire to the county council, where his talents will find their proper scope. A member of this house who allows the real or fancied needs of his province to dominate his national sentiments should seek a field of endeavour where his bias would be less harmful and more appreciated. At this point I should like to say even more emphatically that the member of any provincial legislature who uses his power in an attempt to enhance his own prestige at the expense of national unity is no patriot, be he malicious, or ignorant, or vain, or all three.

Party government is no bar to national unity. On the contrary it is perhaps its strongest binding tie. This can be true only so long as party lines divide this country horizontally. Vertical lines of division are lines of sectionalism and of selfishness and that way lies disaster. He is no patriot who
pits east against west, the centre against the far-flung frontiers. That way lies chaos, dissension and defeat.

If Canadian politicians had spent one-tenth of the time and effort in educating the various parts of Canada as to their dependence upon each other that they have spent in provoking sectional antagonisms for selfish political ends, I venture to say that this great Canadian problem would hardly be a problem to-day. But we ask ourselves, ""Is it a paramount question?"" When we admit that it is, then we ask ourselves, ""Why?"" It is a problem because it affects the rights and privileges, the opportunities and rewards of every citizen. It is a problem because the very physical structure of the nation is threatened. It is a political question, an economic question and a social question. It touches every side of life of every citizen.

We come then to this question: Having recognized that there is a problem and having admitted that this house is the logical place where it should be dealt with, we then ask, ""What are we to do?"" I venture to say that no one can answer that question; there is no all-embracing answer. Most of us have come to realize that when we meet a man who knows all the answers, we have met a fool or a fanatic. We must then begin by laying down such fundamental principles as will guide us in arriving at a judgment on the various methods we shall explore. We must first realize the implications of national unity and we must then desire to achieve it. Then with knowledge and desire behind us, we must examine eveiy question of national policy in the light of that knowledge and desire. I do not hesitate to say quite frankly that in my opinion policies in Canada have always been influenced more by constituencies than by principles. Perhaps this can be more readily illustrated by a study of Canadian tariff history than in any other way.

I have said that Canadian tariff policy has been influenced more by constituencies than by principles. I propose to show that the practice is accepted without comment by the very persons who suffer most from tariff instability. I quote from Canadian Business of December, 1937, which, speaking in advance of this session, says:
It looks also as if the prairie tariff talkers will get a hearing on textiles, furniture and automobiles.

No suggestion that the government might be considering the needs and wants of the Canadian consuming public if, as the article suggests, it is planning a step along the Liberal way. ""Oh, no,"" says Canadian Busi-
The Address-Mr. Mutch

ness, ""if it comes it will be a sop thrown to the prairie tariff talkers, those strange western representatives of the poor rural rustics who believe that the duty of governments is to legislate for the people and who, incredibly enough, say so in public."" This is another quotation from the same publication:

It is unlikely the apple preference of $1.50 per barrel will be disturbed for it is a life and death proposition for the Annapolis valley and even a reduction in it would probably compel the Minister of National Revenue, Hon. J. L. Ilsley, to find a new political address.

Hon. members will notice that the story stresses, not the principle of tariff adjustment, not the economic situation in the Annapolis valley, but'-the climax for Canadian Business-the possible reelection of the minister. I cannot fail to take issue with Canadian Business on this point. Without exonerating this or any other Canadian government from political consideration when tariffs are tinkered with, I feel sure that the hon. minister in question would throw away his seat, and mine too, rather than abandon his convictions.

Finally, there is another feature of the importance of national unity which should never escape the notice of the house. All of us are constantly made aware of our duties as citizens and we should give some thought to our rights. We share a common heritage and we owe a common duty, not only to the state but to each other and to ourselves. As Canadians we have decided that certain standards and services shall be maintained. By no stretch of the imagination can we justify discrimination as between Canadians in the enjoyment of these standards and services. The origin of these services is not local, their importance is not local and the advantages accruing are not local-they are national. By every test and upon every consideration, the responsibility is upon this house. If we meet it, we shall go a long way toward the goal of an harmoniously united Canada.

At this point I cannot do less than express my satisfaction that the speech from the throne foreshadows one step in the right direction, that of unemployment insurance. Here too I might pay my tribute to the government of the day for the appointment of the royal commission. In my opinion and in the opinion of the majority of my constituents, this commission has undertaken an herculean task. I believe that the government has selected men who are equal to that task.
There is another great problem which touches on the happiness and well-being of our people. This is a twin problem, the problem of housing and the problem of slum clearance.

As I have said, this is a national problem and out of it spring many of the social problems which we have to face. Although not mentioned in the speech from the throne, I trust it has not been forgotten. Of this I shall have more to say at another time.

Second only to the problem of setting our national state in order is the problem of determining what our position is to be with relation to the other nations of the world, and what steps we shall take to maintain that position. These are troublesome times in the world at large. I submit it is not too much to say that the conscience of man has been dulled. There has been a futile scurrying from one untenable position to another in connection with international affairs. This so-called diplomacy of another generation has been perpetuated in this newer age. We are stumbling along the old paths, unwilling but surely. For all of this, this government is hardly to blame. Our opportunity for world leadership is limited both geographically and numerically. We are too far from the seat of discord and too weak to be a threat to those who transgress human rights. Yet I could wish that we in Canada stood more foursquare to our problems. To my mind, we have done something, but not enough.

The challenge to leadership was never more clear, more decisive or more urgent. Beginning with the deliberations at Versailles and continuing until to-day the outmoded statesmen of the world have floundered. They have played safe when audacity would have won the day. They have feared when courage might have swept the field. They have compromised when there was nothing to gain. The criticism which I make of the governments of the world, including our own, is that none of them really faces up to the fact of a changed world. None seems to realize that despite the alarms of war this is the hour to strike for peace.

Peace is or ought to be the greatest achievement of mankind. Its importance transcends the importance of liberty, prosperity and power. Without peace these are nothing. We have heard that there can be no peace without honour. Perhaps we ought to reverse those words and say that there can be no honour without peace. Without peace honour is hollow and meaningless. We have been contemptuous of those who cry for peace at any price, failing to realize that without peace price has no substance.

The tragedy of humanity is that we learn so slowly. Our elders, usually dominant in the affairs of the world, proceed with the caution that comes with experience and disappointment. In a fast changing world they
The Address-Mr. Mutch",,,,

1131938,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.12.1.3,1938-02-07,,,,stagedirection,,,,"miss all too often the tempo of the hour. Someone has said that to achieve greatly, one must dare greatly. The world has failed in that; we have kept our feet on the beaten paths which for centuries have led again and again to failure and despair. We need to explore the by-paths; we need to pioneer new trails.

We in Canada are a young nation and we ought to be vigorous, imaginative and courageous. We ought to face the world with something of the attitude of Pitt. You will remember, sir, that the great Walpole had chided Pitt for his youth and rashness. We ought as a nation to ponder on Pitt's reply. He said, ""The atrocious crime of being a young man, which the hon. gentleman has with such spirit and decency charged upon me, I shall neither attempt to palliate nor deny; but content myself with wishing that I may be one of those whose follies may cease with their youth, and not of that number who are ignorant in spite of experience.""

Asquith's policy of ""wait and see"" produced the crisis that made Lloyd George the man of the hour. But, sir, the old policy of muddling through is out of step with the times. Events move too quickly in this day and generation. Neither the Canadian people nor the Canadian government can afford to merit the description of those in Dante's hell, ""The wretched souls of those who lived without or praise or blame.""

We have had some inkling of public reaction to those who dare to be definite even when they dare to be wrong. The public of Canada is tolerant of the mistakes of those who would come to grips with our problems.

We in this house are, I believe, capable of expressing the mind of our people, and I hope that from this session of parliament there may go out a reasoned, imaginative, courageous expression of opinion on foreign relationships which will be a guide to our government, an answer to the question, ""How long^ halt ye between two opinions?"" and an inspiration to the world. But, sir, the great tragedy of the ages is that by the time young men are convinced they cannot right the wrongs of the world by their own wisdom, they have become so old that they regard it as hopeless. I wonder if any man who has not, face pressed to earth, felt his insides turn to water as the bombs came whistling down, is competent' to evaluate the claims of humanity as against vested interests in the game of war.
It will be asked, What could, what can Canada do in the world scheme of things? Something she can do. Here in this new
world she can, if she be willing to pay the price, raise the standard of national morality, and say with Luther, ""Here I stand; God helping me, I can do no other.""

The United States is half right, and therefore wholly a failure in international affairs. Right when she sees that leadership toward peace cannot be looked for from Europe; a failure because, so far. she has failed to rise to repeated opportunities of leadership. Like the Pharisee she has gathered her cloak about her and passed by on the other side. Our guilt is only less because our opportunities, and therefore our responsibilities, are less.

What can Canada do? If we cannot give leadership to the world we can at least set an example, and who knows but what that example might be strong enough to divert the rolling river of doom that threatens to engulf the world.

I have no language to express my scorn for the hypocrisy of those who are unwilling to fight for peace. I think of those thousands, yes millions, who did not scorn to die for peace. I think again of the poet's words, ""We have kept the faith."" We said, ""We shall go down with unreluctant tread, rose crowned into the darkness."" Is that real to you? I saw it! I stood by while an endless procession passed me one by one, outward borne. What did they die for? They were not professional soldiers doing a job. They had no dream of conquest, nothing to gain, everything to lose; no hatred for their foes, no traditional national enemies held in contempt from childhood; no dream of empire; no old scores to settle, and yet horribly, damnably, they died to a man, doing a job they hated, to free the world from this monster for all time. They died for an ideal, the ideal that may deliver this world for all time from the monster which even then was devouring them. They fought for peace, they paid for peace, and counted death nothing if the end was peace.

Well, they fought their fight, and for a little while we hoped and planned and, more briefly still, we believed. Gradually we began to realize that the fight for peace had not been won. There was wavering in the ranks. The world statesmen began to count the cost of peace, and the price was too high. National pride became an obsession, at the expense of national honour, national decency. Avarice outweighs principle; madmen speak and millions tremble in fear. It is not a pretty picture; it is not a hopeful prospect, but, sir, it is not yet hopeless. Perhaps it., is now the eleventh hour; but there is, one ventures to think, even yet, one hour for repentance. It is not too late to say that,
The Address-Mr. Mutch
come weal or woe to our physical being, we have counted the cost and we will pay the price of peace, and I venture to say that the price of peace will be no dearer than the price of folly.

In this dark hour how shall we, being both British and Canadian, answer the challenge, ""Stands England-stands Canada-where she did?"" We know the bitter answer. Let us in all humility start afresh to be once more a nation, new, vigorous, neither ignorant of our destiny nor unwilling to pay the price of its realization. Let us brush aside the cold, dead hand of the past that reaches forth again to lead us by the old pathways to the ever-yawning abyss. Let us be definite, clear-cut and courageous, wrong sometimes, if that is the price we must pay for forthrightness, but moving forward always, building on our errors to be more often right. Above all, let us rise above the ultimate in hypocrisy-agreement in principle and denial in practice.

This brings me to the question of how we are to maintain our national integrity. Sir, it seems to me-and I have said so before in the house-that ten millions of people cannot long hope to hold half a continent in an overcrowded world. It is our good fortune that Canada abounds with those things which the world wants and must, in many instances, have. It is a noble heritage but it involves a great responsibility.
We must examine three possibilities. First, we may simply drift until, as the inevitable result of such a policy, we are invaded and overrun. We may then find our destiny among our conquerors.

Or we may proceed with vigour and intelligence to populate our country and develop it and, by trade, supply our world neighbours with their needs, at the same time enriching our own lives. Having brought in and assimilated another ten or twenty millions of people we may then have some assurance that we can indeed protect our shores, our homes, our heritage.
We must, then, it would seem, either populate our country or fight for it, or give it to someone else strong enough to fight our battles, as the price of our defence.

There is a third alternative to drift or immigration. That, sir, is the policy we are following to-day. Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the policy of to-day is partly drift and partly the third policy, which I shall call the policy of limited ""preparedness."" We have progressed to a point where we admit that since we have doors, we might as well have locks; since we have guns, we might as well have ammunition; since we have both, we might as well train
a few men to use them. And, of course, since we have so many generals we have to have some soldiers to keep the generals out of politics or other mischief.

We are united on this, that we will defend ourselves, if need be; but we are quite far from a unanimous realization that the need may come. We are reasonably united in opposition to wars of aggression, but far from united on the question of where our defensive frontier lies. We consent to a limited permanent force for defensive purposes but are quite unwilling, so far, to make the conditions of service such that they will attract to the service men who would by their enthusiasm and ability give us more of military efficiency and of protection for the taxpayer's dollar than we have been getting. I mean to cast no slur upon those who serve us now. Their character, and in most cases their ability, do them credit. Many of the conditions under which they serve do us no credit. We have not received the most or the best for our money. On this point it is noteworthy that in England a similar situation has been recognized and is being remedied. On that subject, when the estimates come up I may have something further to say.

Fnally I turn to the question which is in many ways the most serious and certainly the most pressing problem of them all in that part of the country from which I come. Nobody could be more gratified than I am with the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) this afternoon. And yet, after over seven years, seven long lean years, we are still trying to delude ourselves into believing that unemployment is municipal and provincial, whereas since 1930 it has been definitely a national problem-national in the most real sense of the word. The unemployed who walk the streets of Winnipeg and Edmonton are just as much the problem of Hamilton and Moncton as they are of Winnipeg and Edmonton. But we have failed to realize this or to act on the realization.

The policy laid down in 1930 to 1935, and followed since 1935 by this government, has been wrong in principle and disastrous in its effect. Municipal and provincial governments have been beggared and bankrupted to no avail. What have we done? First of all we have bankrupted both municipalities and provinces in at least four of the nine provinces and impaired the credit of the others. We have forced on to the relief rolls not only the unemployed but all of the unemployable who at the beginning of this time might have been reasonably considered a charge upon the municipal and provincial governments. Then we have loaned the money, in many instances
The Address-Mr. Mutch",,,,

1131939,ca.proc.d.1938-02-07.12.1.4,1938-02-07,,,,stagedirection,,,,"all of it, to maintain this monstrous burden. Recently this government has realized the unwisdom of confusing unemployed and unemployable. Alas, the realization comes too late. We now propose to shift to the local authorities a responsibility which was, perhaps, always rightly theirs but which they escaped in the general confusion of unemployed and unemployable. The catch is that we are too late. The policies followed thus far have already beggared and bankrupted the lesser governmental bodies; they cannot carry any more.

There is the situation as far as that part of the country from which I come is concerned. We need not lay the problem at the door of the Minister of Labour or any other member of the government. We have been reminding them in the morning and in the evening and at the rising and the setting of the sun, for some time. There is a place, and this is the place, where I have the opportunity to say this, and I say it. I believe it, and I shall continue to urge it until some one else replaces me or something is done about it. I am persuaded that the long range policies of this government are sound, that they present the only workable solution of the main problem of employment. I do think that they proceed with hesitating steps in the carrying out of some of these policies, chiefly in the lowering of living costs and increasing of trade by lowering the vicious tariff rates still in effect.

So, sir, I must say with regret that when we come to the short range policies for the immediate relief of a problem which is human and national rather than economic, I feel we have not lived up to the measure of our opportunity. At the same time, loyal to this mistaken concept of local responsibility, we have in reality loaned and lost money which, used otherwise, might have saved those local governments from their present plight.
If I have spoken frankly, that is my nature. If I have offended any, this is my defence.-I find it in Pope's Essay on Criticism:
Fear not the anger of the wise to raise,

DOUGLAS (Weyburn):,,193S,,,"Having read very carefully the speech from the throne, foreshadowing, as it is supposed to do, the government's legislative program for the coming year, I feel in duty bound to the people who sent me here to vote for the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). We desire respectfully to express regret that the speech from the throne does not indicate
[Mr. Mutch.J

that the government has taken or contemplates taking efficient measures to deal with unfavourable economic conditions in Canada, and that no legislative action is proposed to deal effectively with the prevailing uncertainty and insecurity resulting from the inadequate incomes of large numbers of our people.

Every hon. member will naturally think in terms of the people he represents; and I am supporting this amendment because I can find nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that the government is taking, or contemplates taking, any constructive measures to ameliorate the sufferings of the people whom I represent. Nor am I thinking only of my constituents, because the problems that are confronting them are also confronted by nearly a million people living in the drought area and, in more or less degree, all the people living on the prairie. From time to time hon. members in this corner of the house have endeavoured to depict the conditions of the people on the prairie. We have been told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we were cranks, that we were gloom-spreaders. At one time we were told that we did no service to western Canada by painting so black a picture. But I submit that we have been vindicated during the past few months, for the western provinces have submitted through their respective governments to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations briefs which have painted pictures equally black or more so than any for which we in this corner of the house have been responsible.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) outlined the Manitoba situation very well the other day, and I have no doubt hon. members from Alberta will do the same for their province. It is therefore my intention to summarize very briefly the material contained in the report which was made by the Saskatchewan government to the royal commission. May I remind the house that what I am quoting from is not the ravings of some dyspeptic pessimist but a report made by a Liberal government which until a very short time ago was led by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Whether, due to his absence, they have become more intelligent or more progressive I know not. But they have made a report. While I do not agree in all its details with that report, I do think it is very commendable and gives a fairly accurate picture of conditions as they are in Saskatchewan.

It deals first of all with the question of debt. The latest figures, given by the government of Saskatchewan on January 28, show that the provincial debt is just a few dollars short of $192,000,000, with a contingent liability of over $32,000,000, making in all a debt of
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)

over $220,000,000 to be borne by a population of about 900,000. The seriousness of this can be realized when we remember, as the Saskatchewan government pointed out to the commission, that fifty-two per cent of their ordinary revenues were devoted at that date to the payment of interest charges; in other words, that fifty-two cents out of every dollar they collected went to pay interest and forty-eight cents out of every dollar went to pay for education, government administration, relief and other social services. They pointed out that the municipal debt was: For rural municipalities, S61,000,000; for villages, $2,000,000; for towns, $7,000,000; for cities, $57,000,000, or a total of $127,000,000, to be paid by municipal bodies whose incomes are steadily diminishing, while their responsibilities are yearly increasing. That is not the statement of someone trying to overdraw the picture; it comes from the editor of the Regina Leader Post, a supporter of the Liberal party. The housing conditions of these people are such that one could not take time to describe them, but I will give a quotation from a report of the bureau of statistics:

The large six room dwelling is predominant in the maritimes and Ontario where there is least evidence of crowding and conversely on the prairies where four room dwellings predominate, there is definite evidence of inadequate living space, particularly in rural areas. . . . Over 60 per cent of prairie rural homes contain four rooms or less, while the number of such homes in Ontario is less than 23 per cent. In Alberta and Saskatchewan there are more rural households occupying two rooms than in any other room group.

The Saskatchewan government submitted figures to show that in regard to household comforts in rural homes Saskatchewan ranks among the lowest in the matter of farm conveniences and has the unenviable distinction of having fewer homes with sanitary conveniences and running water than any other province in the dominion. The effect, as the result of these long years of unvaried diet and living on starches, has been to reduce the powers of resistance of great masses of these people. When we realize that the maximum relief for a family of five is $20.20 per month, with 15 per cent deduction if they have meat, 10 per cent deduction if they have dairy products, 10 per cent deduction if they have vegetables, we can readily understand that the problem of health, the problem resulting from undernourishment and malnutrition is a very grave one indeed.

This brief points out that not only have the people on relief been affected, but the rest of the people have had their incomes seriously curtailed. Storekeepers, doctors, workers in towns and villages, ministers of the gospel- all these people are still endeavouring to cany on the services of the community, in many cases with resources exhausted, and they can carry on only under great privation and hardship. And no group have suffered more than the school-teachers, particularly the rural teachers. The brief points out that in 1936 the total salaries paid the school-teachers of Saskatchewan amounted to about half what was paid in 1926, and the total of salaries owing to the teachers was about $1,000,000. It proceeds to set out some of the causes, three main causes being mentioned. I cannot deal with them extensively, but it is interesting to note that drought is not given as one of the main causes.

I have listened to hon. gentlemen opposite telling us from time to time that one good rain or one or two good crops would put Saskatchewan and the prairies back on their feet. That was not the opinion of those who presented this brief. They recognized that drought is a factor which has aggravated the situation, but the causes lie deep down in our economic and social system. On page 1 they say:

It will be most unfortunate for Canada as a whole if fundamental weaknesses in the economy of the western provinces, and in particular of Saskatchewan, are ignored in the belief that prosperity will be assured with a return of normal crop conditions.

And the same view is stated on pages 18 and 46. They cite three main causes; the first is the uneven burden of the protective tariff, and as usual they quote the figures compiled by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) before he became a member of the government. I am not going into that except to say that the government of Saskatchewan pointed out to the Rowell commission that those figures show-and they must have agreed with them-that the benefit Saskatchewan derived from the tariff was $3,000,000 a year, the amount it cost Saskatchewan was $29,000,000 a year, and therefore the loss to the people of Saskatchewan was $26,000,000 a year. Therefore on a per capita basis each man, woman or child gained in benefit $3.55 and paid out $31.71, in other words, the tariff cost each man, woman or child in Saskatchewan $28.16 in terms of too high prices that they paid for the goods they bought, over what they would have paid had they been buying in the markets of the world. They pointed out that western Canada was discriminated against, that they received in benefit only $30,000,000 and that it cost them $86,000,000, being a net loss of $56,000,000 per year to the three prairie provinces. Now I am not going to say whether or not those figures are correct, I shall leave their defence to the Minister of Labour, who is an authority on gathering statistics. But I ask, Why should a Liberal government in western Canada present these facts to the Rowell commission? If there were a Tory government in Ottawa I could well understand them talking about the unequal burden of the tariff, but we have a government here which has for its slogan ""Wider and freer markets,"" a government which has in its ranks the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), whose syndicated articles on freer trade are blazoned from one end of Canada to the other. I listened with interest to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) saying that the

farmers give every fifth hog, every fifth head of cattle, every fifth bushel of wheat to protection. But why tell us that? The same thing is true in regard to the second cause they gave. They say that the monetary policy of the government was such that it had worked a hardship on western Canada. I refer the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) particularly to pages 233 and 237. I shall read only one quotation:

In giving the relief officer a power which is practically dictatorial you give him power to discriminate against individuals. The other evening the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) put this question to us in this corner:

I am certain that my friends^ of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, some of whom come from Saskatchewan, or of the Social Credit group, two of whom come from that province, will not admit that the councils in the municipalities which they represent are composed of men who are cogs in any political machine.

I am happy to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. As a new member perhaps I can appreciate their feelings and emotions more thoroughly
as they stood up to speak than other hon.

members, who in their wisdom and experience, have sat in this chamber for many years. I am sorry I was not in the chamber when the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) told the house he was just completing thirty-five years as a member of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I view with regret the content, or
column5: content, inthe speech from the throne. I am moved to

column1: document to be put forth by a government whose Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), whose ministers and many of whose members have so recently participated in that joyous event, the coronation, and later in the imperial conference of the countries of the empire. What a wonderful clearing house that must have been for ideas and what a diversification of problems to be solved! All of this should have been productive of much. But this government has returned for the third session of this parliament and I submit that the speech from the throne leaves much to be desired.

Canada is faced with a number of problems, at least two of which threaten the very lifeblood of our country. The first to which I shall refer is that of poverty in a land of plenty. The second problem is the apparent desire on the part of some provinces to legislate for themselves and to set up nine separate bodies instead of continuing as the great Dominion of Canada which was handed down to us by the fathers of confederation.
I read from the speech from the throne:

It is gratifying to note that, during the past year, there has been a further substantial advance in Canada's economic recovery. Revenues have reached new levels. Trade with other countries has materially expanded.

I submit that the recovery referred to is much more imaginary than real, and that, if divorced from its dependence upon our participation in the armaments program in which the world is engaged at the present time, there is little net economic advance. I thoroughly concur with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he said, on Wednesday last, that increased revenue was obtained last year largely through the exploitation of Canada's mines for war purposes and that we were avidly selling to both aggressor and defending nations.

During the last few years I have spoken with people who are thinking people, and if I can believe what I hear and what I read, it is the opinion of a great many Canadians that our nation is one of the most materialistic in the world. I am forced to agree that that is so. We pride ourselves on our standard
The Address-Mr. Marsh
of living; but I am convinced that Canada is now putting far too much emphasis on the dollar and not enough emphasis on the man. Our national life is full of evidences of this.

I am sorry to say that our churches are not free from it, though I hesitate to criticize them. Our values are all wrong. Does it not seem to be the veriest hypocrisy that we, living in a country where we have virtually control of nickel and to a large extent control of copper, should sell them to belligerent nations for the purposes of destroying life, while at the same time we hear from the radio, the newspaper and the pulpit appeals by the Red Cross-and God bless the Red Cross-that we send sums of money to one million Chinese boys and girls and old men and women to nurse back to health broken bodies, the starved wastage of war? Does it not seem the veriest hypocrisy that shells and other armaments made of Canadian nickel and copper and sold by Canadian industries to belligerent nations should later necessitate philanthropic giving, to nurse, with Canadian surgery and the use of Canadian adhesive tape, perhaps, the products of our own destruction? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is poor economy and worse Christianity. It is entirely unworthy of the traditions of the Canadian people.

I make these observations after serious thought. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was speaking on Monday last, he pointed out very clearly the importance of Canadians not taking sides, that Canada must observe her neutrality, that public servants must be guarded in their expressions of opinion as to any belligerent. Also I am mindful that the Prime Minister, in reply, concurred in this thought, and I was much impressed by his earnestness when he said:

I do hope that in the course of political discussions in this house during the present session, hon. members will think twice with regard to whatever they may have to say on foreign affairs, and ask themselves whether, in viewr of the attitude which great nations such as England, France and the United States have thought it wisest to adopt, we ourselves should seek to outrun them and attempt some of the things that go much farther than they are prepared to go.

Despite this injunction I am moved to say that the present exploitation of Canada's mines in favour of belligerent nations, of aggressive people at war, is Canada's responsibility. I deplore that I must say it is Canada's guilt.
Also am I mindful of the efforts put forth by British statesmen in the last few years to preserve the peace of Europe. Cannot this government, moved by the high principles of

right, justice and peace, do something to eliminate or at least to curtail the exploitation of our mines in order that shells may be sold to belligerent nations? It should never be hinted or even thought of Canada that she sacrificed her national honour for financial gain.
Neither, Mr. Speaker, am I impressed by the
column5: wasspoken of in the speech from the throne, when I

column11: Mr. Speaker, during the discussion, and you will hear it again, because of necessity it must be spoken. Are we to congratulate the government because they have proved themselves to be the greatest tax collectors in the history of federal governments in Canada? I think not. In

column1: recovery as spoken of in the speech from the throne, why does the sales tax-that much discussed burden which unfortunately falls so largely on the commodities that the man making fifteen or eighteen dollars a week has to buy-remain at eight per cent? Why the tax on sugar? You have heard this before, but in view of the economic recovery, why is that tax still one cent a pound? In view of the surplus in the department of the Postmaster General I wonder why postage is still three cents? The leader of the opposition put the matter in its right category when with ridicule he said, ""Behold the surplus 1"" If recent government action gives any indication of what is going to happen in the next few months it would appear that taxes are increasing rather than decreasing. Otherwise why the increase in the radio licence from two dollars to two dollars and a half? I am not going to belabour the point now; I wish to speak of it a little later.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is unbecoming in a young man, especially a new member, to be intolerant. As we approach years of maturity we should find in ourselves a readiness to stand in the other man's shoes, to look at mutual problems through the other man's glasses, and I hope that as long as I am on the opposition benches I shall not be found continually condemning the government. I am not made that way. Consequently perhaps I may remark that when hon. members who now sit to the right of the Speaker move over, as they will do in a little while, to the left of the Speaker, they will conduct themselves accordingly.
Therefore, realizing that this young country of ours-and how prone we are to boast about its trees, its streams and its lakes, its rivers
The Address-Mr. Marsh

that generate power, the nickel and copper we take from the bowels of the earth, the apples which compare favourably with the best in the world-with all its present wealth and its potentialities, is faced with a menace, an enemy which is stalking through the length and breadth of the land, cannot this parliament unite to banish that monster from among us? His name is poverty.
I come, Mr. Speaker, from the industrial city of Hamilton. Hamilton is the Pittsburgh of Canada, and the finest city in this country.

Perhaps I may be permitted to say to them that civilization has always moved from the east to the west, and there may come a time when ""the desert will blossom like the rose"" and Hamilton will extend its boundaries north, south, east and west, but mostly to the east, and when that time comes, the city of ""Toronto the good"" will perhaps find itself rejoicing in the bosom of a greater and better Hamilton.

We pride ourselves in Hamilton upon possessing a university, and we have a school system that we think is second to none. We have other cultural advantages, but Hamilton is still a city of dinner pails and time-clocks and pay envelopes. Because of our natural geographical location, and because of the fact that we have a fine harbour and good railroad service, as good as the present setup can give us, industry knocks at our door, and we joyfully admit industry. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I am distressed to see the men and women who haunt our streets day by day looking for the job they cannot find. I am distressed also by the great percentage of men and women in the city of Hamilton who are working in our industries, giving an honest day's work and receiving in return a pay envelope that is inadequate even for the bare necessities of life. I am further distressed by the number we have on relief. Our relief system is, we think, one of the most economically operated in Canada, and we are proud of it. But relief is a poor substitute for a job, and it is a terrible impost on the taxpayer who is trying to help out his less fortunate fellow-citizens.

We listened the other day with a good deal of interest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as he told us what the government had done and tried to do in the west. We were gratified to hear that the government had done so much, but we

have also heard from western members who have told us of the spectre of poverty that is marching throughout the west, leaving in its wake destitution, bundles of bones-horses or cattle-wandering on the prairies, little children clothed in burlap, receiving a steady diet of potatoes, and perhaps not that. I would like to say to the members from the west that those of us in the east pay our tribute to you of the west. You have been brave; you have fought manfully. Perish the thought that the east should ever forget the west, or the west ever forget the east! Perish the thought that one province should ever war with another! Perish the thought that this Dominion of Canada should ever disintegrate because of selfishness! But I would like to point out that the government now in power appealed to the electorate in 1935, and said: If you put us into office, you will have the federal government and all the provincial governments of this country of the same political persuasion, and we shall have a cohesion and a unity which will enable us to solve many of the problems that are now distressing this country. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this government stands condemned until that is a realization, and not just a fond hope-and that time is not yet.

To the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) I would suggest that we cannot brag about our trade and commerce so long as we have 960,000 people on relief in a country of 11,000.000, almost one in eleven of our total population. We cannot brag about our resources or our world trade so long as we have a great mass of people in our cities and in the country living in the shadow of insecurity, and of fear of what to-morrow may bring.

May I say a word about the tendency on the part of this government to reduce tariffs in industries which depend upon protection for their very existence, the payrolls of which are even now inadequate to afford a decent living to their workmen. I refer to the reductions that have been made in certain tariffs during 1936 and 1937. I am an advocate of a reasonable tariff for an industry that needs protection. I am an advocate of foreign trade. I believe in exchanging our surplus products, if they can be exchanged with a country whose business cycle is not a feast-and-famine cycle, whose market is more or less stable, whose trade . shows some degree of consistency, and therefore I am alarmed at the reference made in
The Address-Mr. Marsh

the speech from the throne to the proposed trade treaty between Canada and the United States. To what extent will it affect the present British Empire trade agreements, so skilfully and carefully prepared by the late government under its right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett), and implemented by the present government somewhat. There is great apprehension on the part of manufacturers as to what the future holds for them. How can they plan with tariffs that jump around? While the speech from the throne does not indicate the specific classes of goods that may be affected, nevertheless I should like to quote what the leader of the opposition said in his speech on Monday last:

There is nothing more we can give the United States except specific reductions of tariff items, but we are told that what we are to do is to sell our British preference for these benefits. That is the story. Without going into it in detail, the sole, simple question is: What price? And what price means what concessions we are prepared to make from the British preference in order that we may get something for which we have given already everything we have to give on our own account, so that we have nothing more to offer except reductions in specific items. . . . We are not prepared to take quotas when we have given 125,000,000 people everything.

I am rather taken by the undeniable fact- and it applies in this instance-of how history has a habit of repeating itself. Why are Liberal governments against, and why have Liberal governments through all the years been against industry? Senator Beaubien, on April 1, 1936, reviewing the success or failure of reasonable tariff protection of our industries, instanced the year 1930, and said:

So our tariff wall was being demolished brick by brick, and a flood of merchandise from all over the world was pouring into Canadian markets with the result that manufacturers who had been in business in this country for years and gave employment to large numbers of our citizens were unable to withstand the competition.

What was the position in 1930? The manufacturers of the United States, enjoying higher protection and greater sales volume than do our manufacturers, flooded our market with $900,000,000 worth of goods, $600,000,000 worth of which competed directly with our own manufactured products.

I do not say this disparagingly, but it has always struck me as being very strange that, traditionally, the Liberal party has in a sense always been opposed to our manufacturers. My hon. friends opposite know this to be a fact. Why is this?
We are still asking that question in the year of Our Lord, 1938.
The situation was bad enough in 1930. What is it like now? I dare say that there is no other country in the world which provides such

dangerous competition for our industries as does the United States. We could perhaps meet the competition of glassware and boots manufactured in Czechoslovakia, for that country is a great distance from our market, and, so far as its boots are concerned, our people will not wear them. But every hon. member having the slightest experience of business knows that the manufacturers of the United States are competitors against whom it is virtually impossible for us to compete. This was evidenced in 1930.

I shall not read further, but I would point out that since this statement was made, tariffs have again been lowered, and now we have a proposed trade agreement with a country of 125,000,000 people who have protected themselves with a 60 per cent tariff, while our own country, with 11,000,000 people, has an average tariff of approximately 14 per cent. We have an adverse balance of trade with them at the present time; what have we to gain?

It has been said of this government that it is a safe government. I wonder what we mean by ""safe."" We cast our minds back a few hundred years to the middle ages and read of monks going into monasteries in order to be safe. They shut themselves off from the iniquities of the world, from sin, and hardship and warfare in order that they might be safe. We who are in positions of leadership in Canada's parliament are very much at grips w-ith life, and we cannot be inactive; we must wage war on this thing we call poverty. I am mindful that during the recent depression the then government, now sitting in opposition, was blamed for the greatest slump in the history of modern times. The present leader of the opposition, then Prime Minister, came in for a great deal of criticism and blame, but his shoulders were broad. He was blamed for the collapse of the whole world, at any rate for the depression, so far as Canada was concerned. I shall not reciprocate in kind and blame the present Prime Minister and his government for the fact that the sun did not shine at the right time in Saskatchewan; that the rain did not fall; that the wheat did not grow; that men who sowed did not reap. But I do submit, in the light of evidence that we have heard on the floor of the house, that the government did not act soon enough. It did not go into the situation thoroughly enough, and the west

suffered mightily because of the want of aggressiveness and because of the passivity on the part of this government. The government did not act with the dispatch which the pressure of the moment demanded.

And now, I shall voice the protest of hundreds of thousands of Canadians against the present radio situation. First of all, I refer to the increase in licence fee from S2 to $2.50, and in the second place to the impost of $2.50 for each additional radio in the home and for radios in motor cars. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), speaking the other day, hit the nail on the head when he said that it was a nuisance tax and that the people regarded it as such. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was looked upon with a good deal of kindness for a while when it was dependent upon the good will of the people, but it is losing that good will quickly. But there is another question: Why should the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, protected by government licence and supported by the people's funds, go into the radio business on a commercial basis and compete with privately owned radio stations who did the pioneering? Years ago when the radio was a new thing men had faith in it, to the extent of being willing to dig down into their pockets and establish a radio industry. Through the years the going was hard and they were in the red, but now that it appears that world trade is coming back and they have a chance to make money the government goes into the business. What would happen if the government went into the steel business and started to buy and sell steel? You know what would happen, Mr. Speaker, and so do I. This idea, of the government using radio as a commercial means of putting out of business established industry, is wrong.

Might I review briefly why the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was set up? It was established with the intention of providing competition for foreign broadcasts. It was argued that a broadcasting organization supported by the Canadian government, financed by revenues from listeners, and with its credit standing guaranteed by the government, could develop programs which would compare favourably with and therefore could compete with United States broadcasts. These programs were to be made available to Canadian radio stations. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was given wide powers, including power to refuse to any Canadian radio station the right to import any foreign program. I remember well two years ago that a great motor car company which has one of the finest broadcasts on the air desired to send that broadcast over
The Address-Mr. Marsh

Canadian airways. A Canadian radio station had the business initiative, the facilities and salesmanship to go out and sell that company. Then arrangements were made to broadcast the program over Canadian stations, all this to be subject to the approval of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They applied to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and permission was refused. Months later I understand that another motor car manufacturer in the United States, which has a Canadian factory and employs Canadian workmen, wanted to broadcast a radio program in Canada. A Canadian station applied to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the right to use that program, and was refused.

Now what has happened? The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in its search for further revenue is now doing exactly what it formerly would not permit the private station to do for the same purpose. Further, the corporation I understand is offering United States agencies special concessions in the form of corporation networks at a combined cost far below the normal time charges of these stations, also line facilities at less than normal cost. These concessions are being made to attract foreign broadcasts to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stations, and, mark you, the deficit is being paid from my $2.50 and the $2.50 of the poor fellow making $18 a week, who has just as much right to radio as anyone, if our standard of living is to be kept up. Why the right about face?

Now my time is almost up; so let me briefly summarize what I have said about the present radio set-up in Canada. First, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation imports foreign broadcasts for its own network, which privilege has long been denied the private stations. Second, the corporation establishes powerful broadcasting stations but will not permit the private station to increase its power; therefore it cannot compete. Third, the corporation offers sponsors the facilities of ^ these stations, its networks and line facilities, at less than normal cost. Fourth, the non-Canadian activities of this corporation are made possible and the payment of the deficit incurred by a licence fee of $2.50 for each individual radio, which is an imposition and a nuisance tax that should be withdrawn altogether.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have the friendliest feelings for the people of the United States of America-part of my family live there, although they are Canadian born-and I think it is very fine that we can have the friendliest of intercourse with that great English-speaking country. But, sir, I deplore the fact that a
responsible Canadian journal, the Financial Post, can truthfully say, in black headlines, a thing we cannot deny-"" United States speaks-Canada listens!""
Mr. F. D. MacKENZIE (Neepawa); Mr. Speaker, first I offer my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

Then, sir, I wish to speak briefly on one or two subjects that have been discussed during this last week. First, I should like to make some observations on unemployment and relief, chieflj' as relating to the province of Manitoba and more particularly the constituency I have the honour to represent.

Manitoba is still an agricultural province, and as such there will always be a seasonal fluctuation in employment. Under normal conditions there is always a part of the year when employment is active, that is during seeding and still more during harvesting and threshing; also there is a period when employment on the farm is slack. That will always be the case unless there is some change in the set-up, as would now appear to be working itself out, for due to the more extensive mechanization of farming the labour requirements even during the busy season are much less than they were in the past. In spite of that, if it had not been for the help of men from Saskatchewan, Manitoba would have been short of labour during the last harvest season. Farmers from the drought area of Saskatchewan poured into Manitoba last year, and the stream even trickled through to Ontario, as I found in more than one part of this province last autumn. But the fact remains that while in the city of Winnipeg many men were unemployed and on relief the country was short-handed and would have suffered had it not been for the drought in Saskatchewan which allowed the farmers from that province and their sons to come to the assistance of Manitoba farmers.

If we leave out of the picture the drought area in Saskatchewan and Alberta, has there ever been more employment in Canada at this season of the year than there is this year? That does not mean that I am satisfied with the situation; I just put the question. I repeat what I said at the outset, that Manitoba being largely a farming province will continue to have these seasonal fluctuations. Normally more men are required in the summer than in the winter. This has always been the case and will continue to be so under the set-up we have now. What is to be done about the matter? Is the cure to
The Address-Mr. MacKenzie (Neepawa)

be found in establishing more secondary industries in the west? I do not think so, because men employed in factories would not be available on the farms unless the factories worked only in the winter, which of course is not feasible. The cure is to be found in something which will put the farmers in such a financial position that they will be able to hire men for longer periods, that is, to hire permanent help.

In the old days, before the advent of direct relief on the present scale, men went out from the towns and cities to work on the land during the summer months. Then in many cases they went back to the cities, doing little or no work all winter. Some would go to the woods for the winter, but there never has been in Canada sufficient lumbering and allied work to take up the slack of winter unemployment, especially on the prairies. I remember that in Ontario, when I was a boy here, many of the young men in our community would follow the work of sailing on the great lakes. As a rule they did not work in the winter; in the great majority of cases they would lay up. I suppose the nearest we have come to taking up this winter slack in employment in Canada has been during the several railroad building periods of the past.

The point I wish to stress is that before the present period of depression and large scale direct relief, men never thought of going on relief even though conditions in regard to employment were no better than, or not as good as, they have been during the present winter. As hon. members know, people have gone to the cities and gone on relief, and they will not go on the land during the busy season. They prefer to remain on relief throughout the year. In that connection I want to say that the relief rates are so high in the cities that farmers cannot afford to pay men enough to compete with existing rates of relief. That is the case as between Winnipeg and rural Manitoba. I know a great number of cases in my own constituency, where men have come out from Winnipeg for harvest work, good farm labourers, men who should be living in the country instead of the city, because they know farm work better than city work, and who have gone back to the city because they could draw more in relief than they could make by working in the country. They have made that statement quite openly. A farmer cannot pay wages high enough to compete with the relief rates in the cities at the present time.
That is one side of the situation. There is another side to look at. During the last few years in the west the farmer has taken

such a beating year after year that he has no reserve left. In a great many cases he may be actually gravely in debt. Much of his machinery is in bad repair; much of it is out of date, long past the time for replacement. Buildings are in need of paint and repairs, but the farmers are not in a position to hire men for the better part of the year. They have been hiring men only when they could not possibly get along without help, particularly for harvesting and threshing. Many have done without help altogether. Now that times are a little better for the man on the land, he may put some of his surplus into the new machine he needs so much. Then he may put a little into much needed repairs to his buildings. After that, if his taxes are paid, he can begin to think of hiring help for longer periods of time. Many of the farmers in our constituency would hire men if they were sure they would be able to pay them after harvesting their crops. That is what they have told me. That is why in Manitoba, and especially in our part of the country where a fair crop was harvested last year, some farmers did not hire help except for harvesting and threshing. Last summer they found it difficult to get men in the busy season, having waited too long. This was Where the Saskatchewan men who came into the province at that time saved the situation.

It does create a problem when the farmers do not hire men right through the season but take them on for only short periods. First, it makes it difficult for the farmer himself to have any choice in his labour supply, for when he does need a man the supply is limited. In the second place it is very difficult for the labourer to carry on until he is again needed on the farm, and if he finds another job in the meantime he cannot be expected to throw it up in order to work for a few weeks on the farm.

The solution for this phase of the problem will be found only when the farmer himself is assured of a Living wage, an income suited to his requirements. When you assure the farmer a fair return for his work you will automatically solve a great many of the other problems that are worrying us to-day. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) is right; put the primary producer on his feet and you will cure most of our economic ills.

To sum up that part of my argument, if Manitoba is to remain a farming province the position of the farmer must be improved, because labour cannot be employed unless the farmer can afford to hire labour con-
The Address-Mr. MacKenzie (Neepawa)
tinuously. So the farmer must be helped to attain a position where he can hire labour steadily.

Before leaving this point may I say in passing that there are a great many other families who, like the farmers, have fallen behind during the years of depression, and who will find it difficult to exist until they can again find steady employment at reasonably good wages. Many have used up what reserves they had, and at last have had to go on relief. Many, I know, have gone on fighting and have kept off relief. Many of those people deserve a better fate than a continuance of that grim struggle, and I think the government should do more rather than less in providing work for those who have kept off relief in spite of everything.

I should like to offer a suggestion to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) which will help in Manitoba. It is that public works coming under the dominion-provincial agreement, such as road work, should get under way earlier in the season and not late in July or August, as has been the case in the past. I know it is not the fault of the minister; but if that could be done, once seeding is finished men could go to work on the road projects. Then, these being completed, the harvest would come along and the farmers would be able to get men, while the men would continue to get jobs. This would do away with the conflict as between the farmer and the contractor for men for short periods in the summer and the resulting periods when neither the farmer nor the contractor is busy.

There has been an improvement in the Manitoba farm situation, but there is much leeway to make up. Several years like 1937 would do a great deal to put the country on its feet, provided other things were taken care of by the government. This brings me to another matter which has been discussed in the course, of this debate and which I hope to have an opportunity of dealing with at greater length later in the session. It follows naturally and logically.

The speech from the throne mentioned the pending trade treaty between the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada. If I may judge from a survey of Canadian newspapers, there is little opposition to the treaty and much support. The treaties already consummated by this government and the moderate reductions that have been made in the tariff have been generally conceded to have assisted in building up our external trade to the point where we are in fourth position in the world in export trade. That that improved

trade has had a beneficial effect on our whole national position is borne out in many ways and is so stated by many who are not avowed free traders. Mr. Wilson, President of the Royal Bank of Canada, had the following to say in his annual statement:

Where the recent prosperity in the United States has been dependent mainly upon large-scale government deficits, the Canadian recovery took its origin from foreign trade. There was no single remedy to bring about improvement.
He mentions a number of possible remedies and then goes on:
But these should be combined with exceptional efforts on the part of the government to open the doors to foreign markets.
And again:
I view with satisfaction the present tendency among democratic countries to break down barriers impeding the natural flow of business.
He says a lot more which I shall skip. I should like to quote a report in the Ottawa Journal of January 28 of a speech by Mr. McLeod, President of the Bank of Nova Scotia, as follows:

During 1937 there was a modest reduction in the barriers to international trade. Some countries, of which Canada was one, made significant if moderate decreases in their tariffs. New trade agreements were negotiated, of which that between Great Britain and Canada was among the more important. Some exchange controls were relaxed and according to League of Nations authorities the actual administration of such controls and clearing agreements was in many countries made less rigid.

Now that the recovery in trade appears for the moment to have been interrupted, it is more important than ever that further steps should be taken to lower barriers which still obstruct the flow of goods from one country to another.

The recent opening of trade negotiations between Great Britain and the United States is of the greatest significance. A treaty between these two countries would tend to reduce the barriers to trade over a very large part of the world. A truly successful agreement would hold vast promise for the further revival of trade and thus for the continuance of world recovery.

Mr. Speaker, it all seems very reasonable and very logical. Moderate tariff reductions by Canada would be followed by increased trade which would be followed by improved conditions of employment. All this would be to the general benefit of Canada. Does this not suggest that the reasonable and logical course to pursue is the further lowering of tariffs which would be followed by a further improvement in employment and in Canada's economic position? Mr. McLeod goes on to say:
The price of success is a willingness to make concessions in the spirit of give and take, not only by the two parties directly involved but also by Canada and the other British dominions.
The Address-Mr. Betts

These two men cannot be accused of being free traders and yet they ask us to press on to lower tariffs in order to promote the common good of all. We can do this by trade agreements and we can do it in the ordinary way.

We look forward to the agreement mentioned in the speech from the throne with hopeful anticipation. We look forward to further reductions in our tariff structure so that improvement may continue until national prosperity is assured.

As I said before, a few more years like Manitoba had in 1937 would help to put the country on its feet. Two sections of my constituency were completely hailed out and of course the people suffered as a consequence, but the rest of the country enjoyed a comparatively good year. My constituency embraces one of the finest farming districts in the west, in fact anywhere in Canada, sloping as it does to the south and east from the Riding Mountain plateau. Each year of the three I have been a member of this house I have listened to eulogies on the county of Peel, a fine county which I know personally, but if the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray-don) would come west and visit with me for several days I could show him a constituency the equal of his own in many ways, and the superior in others.

I could show him the district which produces the cream and butter which has for years led the province of Manitoba to the grand championship of Canada at all the large fairs. Manitoba has led all Canada since 1924 in the production of quality butter, and for the last several years the creameries of my constituency have led Manitoba to victory. Not only has the Gladstone creamery won the grand championship at the Canadian National Exhibition, but at the last three successive Royals it has captured supreme honours. It has taken those honours right from the front door of the county of Peel.

We also produce live stock which has competed with success at the larger fairs. What is more, our men and boys know their live stock. Of the Manitoba boys' and girls' clubs team at the Royal last year, the four boys in live stock judging were from my constituency. Our honey is of a much better quality than one can find here in Ontario, so much so that I bring my own supply with me each session.

But we have more than fine grain, live stock, butter and honey; we. have admittedly some of the finest scenery in the country. I would like to take hon. members to the Riding mountain national park, down the east slope of the mountain. As the road winds slowly downward through the poplar,

spruce and birch, now on the edge of a precipitous cliff, now overlooking a deep ravine, we would see far below mile after mile of cultivated farm lands and away on to where the far horizon blends into lake Manitoba's waters. Some of those glorious vistas are comparable in kind and beauty, but more expansive, with some we have known in Italy. There are many other scenes which might well make one. on viewing them, imagine himself in bonnie Scotland.

But my time is going and I should like to touch on just one more of the subjects mentioned in the speech from the throne. It gave me pleasure to note that there was to be an expansion in the program of youth training. That is as it should be. The work last year was to some extent in the nature of an experiment, but it proved so successful in our province that its extension is amply justified. I do not know just how much the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will expand or extend his program, but he can be assured of my complete support even to the limit of the greatest burst of generosity by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I do not intend to say more on this now, but I hope to join in the discussion when it comes again before the house.
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, support the amendment.
