BETTS (London):,,193S,,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my own words of congratulation to those we have heard already to the mover (Mr. Francoeur) and the seconder (Mr. Warren) of the motion now being debated. With most of what they said I am in active disagreement, but nevertheless I should like to felicitate them on the graceful manner in which they performed their duties.

At the outset of my remarks, which will be very brief, I too should like to register, as a representative of a riding in which a great many people are engaged in the manufacture and distribution of radios, a strong protest against the increase in the radio licence fee. This added tax, to my way of thinking, is objectionable for a number of reasons. In the first place, it will retard the sale of sets, particularly what are described as secondary sets, that is the small sets, such as are used on the mantel, and in a motor car. In the second place, it is going to place on the Canadian radio audience a burden which is entirely disproportionate to the benefits, if any, that we derive from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Finally, it is a tax which invites evasion and dishonesty, in that the honest taxpayer will declare his
The Address-Mr. Betts

extra sets and pay the very considerably increased tax on each one, while the dishonest taxpayer will conceal his extra sets and evade the tax. Last, and most important of all is the consideration that by this additional impost the government is seriously obstructing an inexpensive source of amusement, relaxation and education which in the past has been available to hundreds of thousands of people in this country who because of their limited means would otherwise enjoy the minimum of these blessings. For these reasons I feel the government might as well cancel the increase at once.
I should like to read the paragraph in the speech from the throne which states:

The strains and stresses, which economic and social developments since confederation have placed upon Canada's governmental structure, have disclosed the necessity for adjustments which will enable it the more effectively to serve provincial and national needs, and to promote and preserve Canadian unity.

With that statement, Mr. Speaker, no one can be in disagreement, and I would venture to suggest to the government of the day a few methods by which the strains and stresses under which we are suffering may be, in part at least, lessened, by which the national need can be better served, and by which Canadian unity may be promoted and preserved.

There is one means which would go a long way towards these very desirable ends, and that is based upon the fact, which we all admit, that to-day we live in an age when propaganda is more powerful and more prevalent than ever before in the world's history. The spoken word and the written word have more power to-day than they have had at any time in the past. That being the case, any measure which will tend to facilitate the means whereby our national hopes, our national problems, our national aspirations, are disseminated will be a measure tending to preserve and promote Canadian unity, and any measure which makes against the establishment of a Canadian literature will be very much opposed to these objects.

I should like to point out that when the former government was in office there was, until 1935, a tax on magazines entering this country from the United States. That tax was removed when the present government assumed office, and the result of its removal has been a tremendous influx of publications, periodicals and magazines, in which the Canadian viewpoint finds no place whatever. Many of them contain a great deal of active proAmerican and anti-Canadian propaganda. Most of them are, to use a colloquialism,

tripe, devoted in the main to cheap sensationalism and pallid pornography. Many of them are decidedly harmful and objectionable, taking into consideration the fact that many of these publications inevitably fall into the hands of our young people. To show the rate of increase of this undesirable type of literature, in 1935 when the duty was on, we imported United States magazines to a value of S2.625.000. The tax was removed, and next year the total value jumped to $4,037,000; last year it was up to 85,900,000. I made some inquiries recently, Mr. Speaker, of a very large and very reputable concern, whose business is the distribution of magazines and publications, and I find that they listed and carried in their stock what they described as

column2: titles""; that is to say, 1,000 separate magazines and periodicals. Of these only 2^ per cent were Canadian; some 35 to 40 per cent originated in the British Isles, and the balance, or roughly 60 per cent, were of United States origin. That is a situation which the government could very readily and simply correct, and I would urge the government in the interests of Canadian unity, with the idea of encouraging our people to do more Canadian reading and more Canadian thinking, to reimpose that salutary tax which existed in 1935.

column1: Another effective manner of promoting Canadian unity is to foster and protect to an adequate extent our Canadian industries. I am not one who is opposed in any sense of the word to foreign trade, nor are such views held by the party of which I have the honour to be a member. But I do appreciate the immense importance to this country of our domestic and imperial markets. Coming from a riding which, as I have said, is industrial, I have seen for myself the benefits which industrial workers there and in every part of the dominion have derived from the empire trade agreements of 1932. Those agreements are just as good as they ever were, and I submit to the government with all the emphasis at my command that in the revision of the Canada-United States treaty which is now being considered they must do nothing to weaken the empire trade agreements. I urge the government not to give away any of our empire preferences. If they follow my suggestions in this connection they will do much to promote and preserve Canadian unity; they will serve the national need, and they will relieve our body politic of some of the strains and stresses from which we are suffering.
Turning to another paragraph of the speech, I note the mention, and a very proper one,
The Address- Mr. Betts

of the coronation ceremonies. That event has been described as one of special significance, and we are all in entire agreement with that expression. On that occasion our young king and his young queen assumed staggering responsibilities, of which they have since discharged themselves royally and magnificently. On that occasion all parts of the empire were represented. It was the greatest festival of empire the world has ever seen. It was an opportunity for every part of the empire to advertise itself before a great cloud of witnesses. I call to mind the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), with which I am in full agreement, as to the desirability of this dominion advertising its products in London to the very best possible advantage. The coronation ceremonies afforded Canada, along with the other dominions, a golden opportunity of advertising its greatest national product, its manhood. We were honoured along with the other parts of the empire by an invitation to send a delegation to represent Canada.

Let us see how the government availed itself of that opportunity and how they proceeded in their selection of Canada's contingent. In the first place, they made a ruling that representatives should attend the ceremony from our naval, militia and air services and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-an eminently proper riding. A delegation was built up totalling three hundred and fifty-one. It was composed of thirty from the naval services, two hundred and fifty-six from the militia services, thirty from the air services, and thirty-five from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Let me say before I go any further, in order that no misunderstandings may arise, that the representatives of the mounted police, I am told by every one who was at the ceremony, were a credit to their corps, to their commissioner, and to their country. I have heard them described time after time as the smartest uniformed men in the coronation procession.

I propose to deal with the representatives of the militia service-a subject in which I have a particular interest, having served for some time in the Canadian militia. Let us examine that militia contingent of two hundred and fifty-six with the idea of seeing how it was made up as to ranks. It is a question, no doubt, that must have given the government some thought. I shall not weary you, Mr. Speaker, by detailing all the various ranks; I shall simply say that in that contingent there were thirty-two gunners, privates and bandsmen, and the balance of the contingent, two hundred and twenty-four, consisted of officers and non-commissioned 51952-16
officers. I do not know what precedent the government followed in arriving at that quota.

I think it is of interest to see how some of our military formations are made up as far as the matter of rank is concerned, and I would place on the record a few figures as to the constitution of an infantry battalion on a peace-time basis. I take an infantry rifle battalion as being typical. The total of all ranks of such a unit is four hundred and seventy, and of these there are two hundred and thirty-four private soldiers. In other words, as near as a toucher, there is one private soldier for each other soldier of higher rank. I would draw to your attention, sir, that in the coronation detachment, for every private soldier-and I speak still of the militia detachment-there were seven soldiers of higher rank to every private. As a result of that somewhat top-heavy constitution of the militia detachment, some strange things followed. I should like to read an article from The Legionary of July, 1937, entitled ""Tickled Tommies"":

Canadians could be very proud of the military bearing of the dominion's contingent, declared Colonel J. E. L. Streight, M.C., M.P., commandant of the Canadian coronation contingent, on his return from England last month. The Canadian guard at Buckingham palace was mounted with only one day's notice in advance, and it was conceded that the Canadians turned out as smart a guard as the British regulars, Colonel Streight said.
There were one or two amusing incidents in connection with the Buckingham palace guard duty.

Before we mounted guard, sentry duty there had never been done by warrant officers, and a special order had to be issued by the War Office to permit Canadian N.C.O's to perform the duty of a private soldier. It was necessary because of all our contingent of 359 there were only five privates. British Tommies were tickled to see regimental sergeant-majors and other high-ranking warrant officers doing sentry duty like private soldiers,"" Colonel Streight related.

I can only say that British Tommies and others may have been tickled to see an entire reversal of what is usual in important military duties, especially when these duties were being carried out at the king's front door. But if I may speak for many people who were anxious to see the best possible, the most military and the smartest detachment representing Canada on that important occasion, these people-many hundreds of thousands of them-were not and are not tickled by that extraordinary situation. Dealing still with the claim made by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Streight), who commanded the Canadian contingent on the occasion in question, that the Canadian guards were as smart as the British regulars, I would refer hon. members to the coronation
The Address- Mr. Betts

number of the Illustrated London News of May 22, 1937. It is in the parliamentary reading room and they can get it there. There is probably no publication that has a wider circulation in every part of the British Empire than the Illustrated London News, and at page 955 hon. members will find a picture with the following letterpress beneath it:

The first dominion troops to guard the royal palaces: Canadians relieving the Welsh guards. On May 9, for the first time in history, dominion troops mounted guard at British royal palaces. Precedence was accorded to the Canadian coronation contingent as representing the oldest dominion. They took over from the Welsh guards at fourteen posts (seven at Buckingham palace and seven at St. James's palace) for six hours.

If hon. members will examine the picture they will see that it shows a sentry being posted for guard duty, and being instructed in his duty; and standing beside him is the sentry whom he is about to relieve. The sentry who is being posted and instructed is a Canadian sergeant-major, who, as hon. members know, is a very high-ranking non-commissioned officer. He is being instructed in his duties by a Canadian corporal, an extremely junior non-commissioned officer. That, I submit, is making a farce of what should be a solemn occasion, and there was no necessity for it except for the fact that the government chose to leave all privates at home except thirty-two. I make these remarks not with any pleasure whatever, but simply because I regard it as a duty that should be performed. Nor do I know who the sergeant-major is. He may have a fine military record, or a fine political record; I do not know anything about that. But he is not a smart and soldierly figure. His greatcoat is pulled all awry; he stands a foot shorter than the imperial soldier whom he is relieving; and he has a bulge in front, which, to put it mildly, suggests that for a soldier doing sentry duty outside his majesty's palace he is in a very interesting condition.

In all seriousness, I am going to submit to the government that to choose a contingent, in which private soldiers were represented, on the scale of one to seven, is the antithesis of democracy, and the quintessence of fascism. I say further that the adoption of any system whereby the plums go to the high-ranking men, ""and to blazes with the men in the ranks,"" will do more than anything else, not to promote and preserve national unity, but to prevent and to destroy it. It will do more towards that end than anything I can imagine. I would say, furthermore, that it should have been obvious to the meanest intellect; it should have been obvious to the

Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), that the private soldier, the man in the low-paid ranks, was least able to pay his way to this great festival of empire, while the high-ranking officers were best able to go at their own expense.

I remember that in the course of the last election campaign there was a grandiose and grandiloquent book displayed on the newsstands, selling for SI or more. It was called The Liberal Way, and I am told on very good authority by my publisher friends that it can now be picked up in any departmental store for fourteen cents. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, if the manner in which Canada's coronation contingent was selected was the Liberal way, the book is grossly overpriced at fourteen cents. I would not give the Prime Minister's favourite price of five cents for it; in fact, I would not take it as a gift.
On motion of Mr. Turgeon the debate was adjourned.
